bio.en: Rachel Lockett is an executive coach and former longtime HR leader at Pinterest and at Stripe who helps CEOs, founders, and tech leaders with emotional intelligence, resilience, and building trusted, accountable teams.
bio.zh: Rachel Lockett 是一位高管教练，也曾长期担任 Pinterest 与 Stripe 的人力资源负责人，她帮助 CEO、创始人和科技领导者提升情商、韧性，并打造值得信赖、各负其责的团队。

summary.en: Rachel argues that great leaders don't need to have all the answers; instead they equip their teams by attuning to context and coaching rather than dictating. She shares how to make difficult conversations easier, how technical leaders can avoid burnout by operating in their gifts and strengths, and why seeking help is a vulnerable but necessary step. The episode reframes the 'human side' of building companies as both fun and high-leverage.
summary.zh: Rachel 认为，杰出的领导者不需要掌握所有答案；相反，他们通过体察情境、以教练方式赋能团队，而非发号施令。她分享了如何让艰难对话变轻松、技术型领导者如何借助自身天赋与优势避免职业倦怠，以及为什么寻求帮助虽令人脆弱却是必经的一步。本期将“打造公司的人的一面”重新定义为既有趣又高杠杆的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When clients come to you, what is the biggest gap they have that is keeping them from being successful as leaders?
turns.zh: 当客户找到你时，他们身上最大的短板是什么，导致他们无法成为一名成功的领导者？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Most leaders, especially technical leaders, assume they have to have all the answers. People have climbed the ladder because they've been dependable, reliable, the smartest person in the room. But great leaders know that when you try to advise and have the answer all the time, you're not actually equipping your team to go solve the hard problems. You're training your team to come to you with all of the hard problems.
turns.zh: 大多数领导者，尤其是技术型领导者，都以为自己必须知道所有答案。人们之所以能一路晋升，是因为他们一直都可靠、值得信赖，是屋里最聪明的人。但优秀的领导者明白，如果你总是试图给建议、给出答案，你其实并没有让团队具备去解决难题的能力。你是在训练团队把所有的难题都丢给你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Difficult conversations are difficult. How do we help people make them less difficult?
turns.zh: 艰难的对话之所以难，就是因为它难。我们该如何帮助人们让这些对话没那么困难？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: We operate in tech. We're supposed to give all of ourselves, all of our time, all of our energy to this endeavor, and it's purely logical. That's not at all true. It's completely emotional. Professionals have feelings. People, when they want to have a conflict, they come in ready to prove their point. There's a misguided view that the goal is to convince the other person that what they're doing is wrong. Actually, the goal of any conflict is to create mutual understanding.
turns.zh: 我们身处科技行业。我们本该把全部的自我、时间和精力都投入这项事业，而且一切都应该纯粹是理性的。但事实完全不是这样。它完全是感性的。职场人也是有感情的。当人们想要发生冲突时，他们进来时已经准备好要证明自己是对的。有一种错误的观念认为，冲突的目的就是要说服对方，让他们觉得自己做错了。实际上，任何冲突的目的都是达成相互理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk about what you've learned about helping leaders in tech avoid burnout.
turns.zh: 聊聊你在帮助科技行业的领导者避免职业倦怠方面学到了什么。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: When people are in their gifts and their strengths, they have more energy. We all have more energy when we're operating from the things we naturally are good at. It's no one else's job to help you live in your gifts. What I notice in big companies is people are often annoyed or frustrated with their management for not making their job more interesting. No, your manager's job is to help you perform in the job you are hired to do. It's your job to navigate your career.
turns.zh: 当人们在发挥自己的天赋和优势时，他们会有更多的能量。当我们做自己天生擅长的事情时，都会更有活力。没有人有义务帮你活在自己的天赋里。我在大公司里观察到，人们常常对管理层感到不满或沮丧，因为管理层没有让工作变得更有趣。不对，经理的职责是帮助你在被聘来做的那份工作上表现出色。经营你的职业生涯，是你自己的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The power of this is this makes your life so much better.

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Genuinely, I hope that your listeners take away that the human side of business building is incredibly fun and impactful and that it's easy to do. They can do it with simple tools. So, I'm hopeful that through this conversation, heads of product, heads of engineering, founders walk away feeling more empowered and more motivated to attune to the people around them.
turns.zh: 真诚地说，我希望你的听众能带走一个认知：做业务过程中"人的一面"既极其有趣、又极具影响力，而且做起来并不难。他们可以用简单的工具就做到。所以，我希望通过这场对话，产品负责人、工程负责人、创始人听完之后，会感到更有力量，也更有动力去体察和贴近身边的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what I'm hearing is just if you're struggling with the human side of building a product, building a team, building a company, there are answers. You can do it.
turns.zh: 所以，我听到的是：如果你在产品、团队或公司的"人的一面"上感到吃力，是有答案的。你可以做到。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yes, exactly. It is achievable, and it's actually most natural. Leaders want to care about the people they work with. They want to empower those around them. But sometimes the busyness of our world gets in the way and the urgency of the litany of things to do distracts you from the people in front of you. And actually, if you really understand the talent around you and you create an environment where they can be successful, your business will thrive.
turns.zh: 对，正是这样。这是可以做到的，而且它其实是最自然不过的事。领导者想要关心共事的人。他们想要赋能身边的人。但有时候，我们世界的忙碌会挡在路上，那一长串待办事项带来的紧迫感会让你分心，忽略掉眼前的人。而实际上，如果你真正了解身边的人才，并营造出让他们能成功的氛围，你的业务就会蒸蒸日上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the hardest part of this for people is just there's the knowing this can be helped with. The other is just being vulnerable enough to seek help and to take this on because it's so hard. Just like, "Oh, maybe I'm not a great manager." That doesn't feel good.
turns.zh: 我觉得对人们来说，最难的部分之一就是"知道这事是可以被改善的"。另一部分是要有足够的勇气去示弱、去寻求帮助、去接下这件事，因为这真的很难。就像，"哦，也许我并不是个好经理。"这感觉并不好受。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, that's true. I mean, it's vulnerable to seek help, but I think your audience, I know to be incredibly committed to growth. I hear of people who come on your podcast and they've spent decades focused on self-improvement. And I actually want to tell you a story about one of my clients who loves your podcast, and I was talking to him last week. He's a client I've seen for 10 years, and he's a person who exemplifies a commitment to personal growth. (00:07:08): I started working with him when he was a frontline engineering manager at Coinbase, and we talked about who he is, what his strengths are, and his bigger picture why. And he talked about this dream of creating a global movement one day. He was really focused on building community, and he thought the path for creating possibility in the world around him was creating a strong community around him. And he continually worked on his leadership capacity. And over the 10 years, at some point, he created a tattoo on his arm that's a sun with a redwood grove around it that reminded him of his core strengths and his purpose. And today, guess what he's doing, Lenny?
turns.zh: 是的，确实。我的意思是，寻求帮助是需要勇气的，但我了解你的听众，他们对于成长有着令人难以置信的投入。我听说上过你播客的人，有些人花了几十年来专注自我提升。其实我想给你讲一个我客户的故事，他很喜欢你的播客，我上周刚和他聊过。我跟他合作了 10 年，他是一个把"对个人成长的投入"体现得淋漓尽致的人。(00:07:08): 我刚开始和他合作时，他还是 Coinbase 的一名一线工程经理，我们聊过他是谁、他的优势是什么，以及他更宏大的"为什么"。他谈到有一天要创造一个全球性运动的梦想。他非常专注于建立社群，并且认为，要在他周围的世界里创造可能性，路径就是在他身边建立一个强大的社群。于是他持续提升自己的领导力。在这 10 年里，有段时间他在手臂上纹了一个纹身——一个太阳，周围环绕着一片红杉林——用来提醒自己核心的优势与使命。而今天，你猜他在做什么，Lenny？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.

turns.en: This story reminds me of just why I love these sorts of conversations because the sort of stuff we're going to be talking about, and we'll get into it right after this final preamble, is stuff that's usually locked away in these very small rooms, are only accessible to folks with a bunch of money. This is stuff people pay tens of thousands of dollars, hundreds of thousands of dollars for over the course of their career. And I just love the idea of sharing all this with everyone to help all learn from the stuff that you've learned from all these people you've worked with. So, I'm really excited to be digging into stuff. The first thing I want to dive into, I actually asked you, when clients come to you, what is the biggest gap they have that is keeping them from being successful as leaders? And you told me it's essentially knowing when to coach versus knowing when to just tell people what to do and learning to coach. Talk about what you see there, why this is so important, and how you help people develop the skill.
turns.zh: 这个故事让我想起，我为什么这么喜欢这类对话——因为我们要聊的东西，也就是在这最后一段开场白之后马上要深入的内容，通常都被锁在那些很小的房间里，只有花得起大钱的人才接触得到。这些东西，人们在职业生涯中会花上几万美元、甚至几十万美元去买。而我就是喜欢把这一切分享给所有人，让大家都能够从你曾合作过的那些人身上学到的东西里受益。所以，我真的非常兴奋能深入聊这些。我想先聊的第一件事，其实是我问过你的：当客户找到你时，他们身上最大的短板是什么，导致他们无法成为成功的领导者？你告诉我的核心其实就是要懂得"什么时候该 coaching、什么时候该直接告诉别人怎么做"，以及学会 coaching。聊聊你在这方面的观察、为什么这如此重要，以及你如何帮助人们培养这项技能。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I think that most leaders, especially technical leaders, assume they have to have all the answers. People have climbed the ladder in whatever realm they're in because they've been dependable, reliable, the smartest person in the room. But when you're leading a quickly-scaling company, you quickly have less context than the people you're around. And the way you were operating before doesn't work because you don't have the ability to wrap your arms around every problem in a deep way. So, I've seen leaders at every phase from frontline managers up to running an 8,000-person company struggle with knowing when do I have to have the answer, and when I don't have the answer, what options do I have? (00:10:12): But great leaders know that when you try to advise and have the answer all the time, you're not actually equipping your team to go solve the hard problems. You're training your team to come to you with all of the hard problems. And coaching is a different way. It's an alternative path that unlocks brilliance in your team and is way more motivating for the people around you. So, coaching is actually a learnable skill, obviously, because there's tons of coaches around Silicon Valley, but you don't have to coach in the same way that an executive coaches. You can shift your energy into curiosity when someone brings you a hard problem to solve, and create space to get curious, and help them solve their own problem. (00:10:59): So, obviously, sometimes advising is the right path. If there's an urgent issue, the person coming to you doesn't have the skill they need, that's a time to advise and help. But leaders over-rotate, assuming the people that they've hired who are experts in their domain need them to solve the problem. So, I think it's useful for your listeners to actually know that coaching's an alternative, and I can help them learn some basic skills around this.
turns.zh: 我认为，大多数领导者，尤其是技术型领导者，都假设自己必须知道所有答案。人们无论身处哪个领域，之所以能一路往上爬，是因为他们一直可靠、值得信赖，是屋里最聪明的人。但当你领导一家快速扩张的公司时，你很快就会比身边的人掌握更少的上下文。而你以前那套行事方式也不再奏效，因为你已经没有能力深入地去全面把握每一个问题。所以，我见过从一线经理到管理 8000 人公司的各个阶段的领导者，都在"我什么时候必须给出答案、当我没有答案时我还有什么选择"这个问题上挣扎。(00:10:12): 但优秀的领导者知道，如果你总是试图给建议、给出答案，你其实并没有让团队具备去解决难题的能力。你是在训练团队把所有的难题都丢给你。而 coaching 是另一种方式。它是一条替代路径，能解锁团队里的才华，也更能激励身边的人。所以，coaching 其实是一项可习得的技能，这一点显而易见，因为硅谷到处都是教练，但你不必像高管教练那样去 coaching。当有人带着难题来找你时，你可以把能量转向好奇，留出空间去好奇，帮助他们解决自己的问题。(00:10:59): 当然，有时候给建议才是正确的路径。如果有紧急问题，来找你的人还缺乏所需技能，那就是该给建议、提供帮助的时候。但领导者往往会过度依赖这种"给答案"的方式，以为他们 hiring 来的、各领域的专家还需要他们去解决问题。所以，我认为让你的听众知道"coaching 是一种替代方案"是很有用的，而且我可以帮他们学一些这方面的基本技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we'll link to it. It's this idea that as a leader, people always just coming to you trying to give you their monkey that's sitting on their back. And they're like, "Hey, this monkey is causing me all this problem. I don't know what to do. But this monkey, here you go. You take it, and feed it, and help it, figure out what it needs." And the role of a leader is to keep the monkey on the back of the person and help them figure out how to solve the problem, exactly what you're describing.
turns.zh: 好，我们会在节目里附上链接。它的核心意思是：作为领导者，人们总是来找你，想把他们背上那只猴子交给你。他们会说，"嘿，这只猴子给我带来一堆麻烦。我不知道该怎么办。但你看，这只猴子给你，你拿走，喂它，帮帮它，搞清楚它需要什么。"而领导者的角色是让猴子留在那个人背上，帮他们想办法解决问题，这恰恰就是你说的那样。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, that's a great analogy. I love that. I think leaders make things up when they don't have answers sometimes. A person comes to you with a problem and you just want to help. But the best way to help is actually doing something that most leaders don't do well. It's attuning to what is the context? What does this person need? What are they blocked on? And ask them with those questions so that they can solve their own problem.
turns.zh: 对，这个类比很棒。我喜欢。我觉得领导者有时候在没有答案时会"编"出点东西来。一个人带着问题来找你，你只想帮忙。但帮忙最好的方式，其实是做一件大多数领导者都做不好的事。那就是去体察：当下的情境是什么？这个人需要什么？他们被什么卡住了？然后用这些问题去问他们，让他们能解决自己的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about how to get better at this. But first of all, when you said, "When is it actually smart to just tell them what to do?" You said it's when they don't have the skills to do it. Is there any other kind of heuristics of like, okay, just tell them what to do in these cases?
turns.zh: 我们来聊聊怎么把这件事做得更好。但首先，你刚才说"什么时候直接告诉他们怎么做才是明智的"，你说的是当他们没有相应技能的时候。还有没有别的经验法则，比如"好，这种情况下就直接告诉他们怎么做"？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, it's an urgent issue and you actually have an answer that you want to drive. So, don't coach and make it a game. You want your person on your team to guess what's in your mind. That's not a good time to coach. You have something you absolutely want them to do. You know the right answer. You want them to be motivated to go do it. Advise them. Help them see the path. But most leaders over-index on that solution. So, I want to share. Maybe Lenny, I can teach you two skills that I think are the basics of leader coaching-
turns.zh: 有，那就是遇到紧急问题，而且你心里确实有一个想要推动的答案。所以，别在这个时候 coaching、把它变成一场猜谜游戏，让你团队里的人去猜你在想什么。那不是 coaching 的好时机。当你有某件你绝对希望他们去做的事，你知道正确答案，你希望他们有动力去执行——那就给建议。帮他们看清路径。但大多数领导者太过度依赖这种"给答案"的方式了。所以我想分享一下。也许，Lenny，我可以教你两项我认为属于领导者 coaching 基本功的技能——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. I'd love that.
turns.zh: 来吧。我很乐意。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: ... that you can use in your own life tonight with your wife-
turns.zh: ……你今晚就能用在自己的生活里，比如和你妻子——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: She's going to love this.
turns.zh: 她肯定会喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: ... or anyone you operate with.
turns.zh: ……或者任何你打交道的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And hopefully, your listeners can use them too.
turns.zh: 也希望你的听众也能用上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Okay. So, the first skill is active listening. And Lenny, you're probably a good listener because this is what you do for a living is you listen to the people who come on your podcast. But I don't know if you've seen Fight Club. There's a quote, "Most people aren't listening. They're just waiting for their turn to talk."
turns.zh: 好。那么，第一项技能是积极倾听（active listening）。Lenny，你大概是个不错的倾听者，因为你靠这个谋生——你听那些来上播客的人说话。但我不知道你有没有看过《搏击俱乐部》。里面有句台词："大多数人都不是在听。他们只是在等自己开口说话的机会。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolute-
turns.zh: 绝对的——

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: This is rampant in tech. And great leaders flip that script and tune in. They're the kinds of leaders who walk into a room, and they can see the elephants. They can name them. They can ask the hard questions to get people collaborating. So, there's actually three levels to listening. So, the first level listening, level one is internal. Let's say you're talking to me about a problem. I'm thinking about the implications of that problem on me. I'm completely distracted with my own inner dialogue. That's level one. Most people go through their world rushed and in level one. Level two listening is focused. So, you're talking to me, and I can repeat back what you're saying. So, I am listening to the words you're describing, and that's typically what happens in a good one-on-one. We're problem solving together and focused on your words. (00:14:46): Level three listening is global listening. So, that's what I'm hearing beneath the words. I'm hearing what you're communicating, not just what you're saying. I see your body language. I notice your tone of voice. I know the context around what you're talking about, and I can reflect back more insight about what's happening than you're aware of because I'm understanding everything you're communicating. So, dropping into level three listening is what great leaders do when they're influencing, when they're selling, when they're pitching a vision, and definitely when they're coaching. So, do you want to try it?
turns.zh: 这在科技圈太普遍了。而优秀的领导者会反转这个剧本，真正调频进入状态。他们是那种走进房间就能看出"房间里的大象"的领导者。他们能点出那些问题。他们能提出艰难的问题，让人们开始协作。所以，倾听其实分三个层次。第一层倾听，level one，是内在的。假设你正跟我讲一个你的问题。我心里在想这个问题对我有什么影响。我完全被自己内心的独白分散了注意力。这就是第一层。大多数人匆匆忙忙地生活，都处于第一层。第二层倾听是专注的。你跟我说话，我能把你说的话复述回来。也就是说，我在听你描述的话语，这通常就是一场好的 1对1 谈话里发生的事。我们一起解决问题，专注于你的话。(00:14:46): 第三层倾听是全局性倾听（global listening）。那是我在话语之下听到的东西。我听到的是你在传达的意思，而不只是你说出来的字。我看到你的肢体语言。我注意到你的语气。我了解你所说内容周围的语境，而且因为我理解你传达的一切，我能反馈出比你自己意识到的、关于正在发生什么的更深洞察。所以，进入第三层倾听，正是优秀的领导者在施加影响、销售、宣讲愿景，以及当然还有 coaching 时在做的事。那么，你想试一下吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Okay. How about this? I'll demonstrate some level three listening. I'm going to ask you a question.
turns.zh: 好。这样如何？我来演示一下第三层倾听。我要问你一个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Uh-oh.
turns.zh: 好。呃——哦。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: You told me earlier, you're a father.
turns.zh: 你之前告诉过我，你是一位父亲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What is it like to be a dad?
turns.zh: 当爸爸是什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. What is it like to be a dad? It's amazing. It's like the most amazing thing I've ever done in many ways. I love it so much. It's also quite challenging at times dealing with setting boundaries and knowing when to just let him do the thing he's really excited about or just saying, "no," and just letting him cry for a while. That's something I've been dealing with recently, but it's like everything people tell you it is basically in every way except the joy is so much higher, so much higher than you hear from other people because people always talk about all the downsides, all the pain and challenges.
turns.zh: 哇。当爸爸是什么感觉？太棒了。在很多方面，它就像是我做过的最棒的事。我太爱了。但有时候也相当有挑战——比如在设定界限、知道什么时候该放手让他去做自己真正兴奋的事，还是干脆说"不"、让他哭上一阵子之间拿捏。这是我最近一直在应对的事，但它基本上就像别人告诉你的那样，方方面面都一样，唯一的区别是那种快乐比别人说的要高得多、高得多，因为人们总在谈论所有的负面影响、所有的痛苦和挑战。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, and I see you when you talk about being a father, initially, I saw you really squirm in your chair. Well, this is a big question. And you looked up and down and kind of avoided my eye contact at first because my sense is you love being a dad, and it's so challenging. It's so tiring. And I'm hearing both of that in your answer. The high joy and the discomfort in having to sleep train, and having to disappoint, and navigating challenging behavior.
turns.zh: 嗯，我看到你在聊当爸爸的时候，一开始你其实在椅子上坐立不安。毕竟这是个很大的问题。你上下打量，一开始有点躲开我的眼神接触，因为我的感觉是：你很爱当爸爸，但它也很有挑战。它很累人。我在你的回答里同时听到了这两面。那种极高的快乐，以及不得不做睡眠训练、不得不让人失望、去应对棘手行为时的那种不适。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nailed it. That was very nice to hear. Clearly, you listened to everything I said and that was a really good example of active listening.
turns.zh: 说得太准了。这听着真舒服。显然，你把我说的每句话都听进去了，这是一个非常好的积极倾听的例子。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What does it feel like to be seen that way?
turns.zh: 被那样"看见"是什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels really nice. It feels really nice to be heard. And it's not just like you're repeating back my words. It's here's what I got out of the level below what you're saying, and the gist, and the bigger picture.
turns.zh: 感觉真的很好。被听见的感觉真的很好。而且不只是你把我的话重复回来。而是你从我说的话下面那一层、从要点和大局上，get 到了我的意思。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, there's some emotional connection when you listen actively, and that took less than a minute. So, what I want to invite listeners to understand is that active listening doesn't mean you're setting up an hour coaching session with every person on your team. No one has time for that. But even in the time you're already spending, just focusing on the other person in a way that is novel and really gives them your full attention so you can see their feelings under what they're saying goes a long way to motivating your team and helping them understand what's actually happening under the surface in this situation.
turns.zh: 对，当你积极倾听时，会产生某种情感连接，而那不到一分钟。所以，我想让听众理解的是：积极倾听并不代表你要给团队里每个人都安排一小时的 coaching 会话。没人有那个时间。但即便在你已经在花的时间里，只要以一种全新的方式专注于对方，真正给予他们你全部的注意力，让你能看到他们话语之下的感受，这就足以极大地激励你的团队，并帮助他们理解当前局面表面之下究竟发生了什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's just so much power in different words, repeating back what they said. That's almost implied in what you're describing. It sounds like... So, I don't know, like a trick they'll see through. But knowing that you're listening to me and you're going to show me active listening, it still feels really nice to just hear back what I said. There's a lot of power in that and it's subtle.
turns.zh: 我觉得用不同的话把对方说的重复回去，本身就很有力量。这几乎是你描述里隐含的东西。听起来像……所以，我不知道，像是个他们能看穿的小把戏。但知道你在听我说话、你会向我展示积极倾听，光是听到自己说的话被反馈回来，感觉还是真的很好。这里面很有力量，而且很微妙。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. Great. Yeah, there's an element of synthesizing what I'm hearing verbally. That's the focused listening part, and then, mirroring back the emotions that I'm noticing.
turns.zh: 对。很好。对，里面有一层是把我听到的内容用语言综合起来。那是专注倾听的部分，然后，是把我注意到的情绪反射回去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The emotions.
turns.zh: 那些情绪。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And even things that I'm guessing, and I can say, "Is that right?" And you can say, "No, actually, I'm not conflicted about the challenges of being a dad. I just am so joyful." And then, now, I understand where you're coming from and so do you.
turns.zh: 甚至包括我去猜测的东西，我可以说，"是这样吗？"而你可以说，"不，其实，我对当爸爸的挑战并不纠结。我只是太快乐了。"然后，我现在就理解了你的出发点，你也一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so this is a core skill of coaching is active listening.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，所以 coaching 的一项核心技能就是积极倾听。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yes. So, that's listening. Second skill, powerful questions. So, asking powerful questions means I'm curious about what's really going on, and there's not one right answer. So, a powerful question helps you gain insight and it takes you to a new solution set you didn't have before. But it's not me leading the witness. I'm not trying to guide you to a specific answer. That wouldn't be a powerful question. So, something that I like to equip leaders with is four kinds of questions that you can ask to unlock insight. (00:19:17): So, the first kind is I use a GROW model. So, the GROW model just is four different categories of kinds of powerful questions. So, the G in grow is goal. So, what does success look like? What's the outcome that you want to have? Any question that's around defining the best case scenario. The R in the GROW model is about your current reality. Where are you stuck? What are your current challenges? What have you tried? The O is about your options. So, let's expand the opportunities that you can understand of the choices you have in front of you. What are the various paths you could take? And the W in the GROW model is the way forward. What are you going to do next? So, this sounds simple, and it is simple if you take the time and space to listen carefully and ask any of these questions. The people on your team will appreciate the space and time to unlock an option that they didn't think of before and walk away with a concrete next step.
turns.zh: 对。所以，这是倾听。第二项技能，有力提问（powerful questions）。提出有力问题，意味着我对"真正在发生什么"感到好奇，而且没有唯一正确的答案。所以，一个有力的问题能帮你获得洞察，把你带到一个之前没有的解题集合里。但我不是在"诱导证人"。我不是想把你引导到某个特定答案。那就不算有力的问题了。所以，我喜欢教领导者用四类问题来解锁洞察。(00:19:17): 第一类，我用的是 GROW 模型。GROW 模型就是四类有力问题的分类。GROW 里的 G 是 Goal（目标）。所以，成功是什么样子？你想要的结果是什么？任何围绕定义"最佳情形"的问题都算。R 是现实（Reality）。你卡在哪里？你目前面临的挑战是什么？你试过什么？O 是关于选项（Options）。我们来拓宽你对自己面前可选机会的理解。你有哪些可以走的路径？W 是前进方向（Way forward）。你接下来要做什么？所以，这听起来简单，而如果你花时间和空间去认真倾听、并提出其中任何一类问题，它确实简单。你团队里的人会感激这段空间和时间为他们解锁一个之前没想到的选项，然后带着一个具体的下一步离开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, just to reflect back what you're saying, so someone comes to you with a monkey on their back. Here's a problem I'm trying to solve. This percent of my team is just not doing something right or this feature isn't working, something like that. So, first of all, it's listen, be very active in your listening. Reflect back what you're hearing, their emotions. And then, ask them questions around what does success look like for this? What is the goal? What is the goal? What does success look like for the thing you're trying to do here? What does success look like? Two is just what's today's reality? What's happening today? Then, options. Here's options that you think exist. So, this is you asking them what are the options?
turns.zh: 所以，把我听到的总结一下：有人背着只猴子来找你。比如，"有个问题我想解决。我团队里这部分人就是做不对某事，或者这个功能不 work 了"，类似这种。所以，首先，是倾听，要非常积极地去听。把你听到的、以及他们的情绪反馈回去。然后，围绕"这事成功是什么样子"去问他们问题。目标是什么？目标是什么？你想做的这件事成功是什么样？成功是什么样？第二，就是"今天的现实是什么"？今天发生了什么？然后，选项。这里是你认为存在的选项。所以，这是你在问他们：有哪些选项？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, what are your paths forward? What could you do next?
turns.zh: 对，你的前进路径是什么？你接下来能做什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What could you do next? And then, this is organic. So, it's not just like one, two, three, four, I imagine.
turns.zh: 你接下来能做什么？然后，这是自然发生的。所以，我想它不只是一、二、三、四那样机械地走。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But the final step is just, okay, what's the way forward? What do you want to do?
turns.zh: 但最后一步就是，好，前进方向是什么？你想怎么做？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That's exactly right. And you don't have to do it in this order. These are just four kinds of questions.
turns.zh: 完全正确。而且你不必按这个顺序来。它们只是四类问题而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see.
turns.zh: 我明白了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: So, you might come and someone's super clear about their outcome. You know that. You don't need to spend any time asking them questions about that. Maybe you just want to really dig in on where are they stuck? And once they start talking about their reality and where they're stuck, then they realize, oh, I'm stuck because my cross-functional partner is blocking me, and I don't have any relationship with them. I need to go meet with them actually and just have a breakthrough conversation, tell them where I'm stuck. So, sometimes talking this out loud, just creating that space for them is going to help them tremendously.
turns.zh: 所以，你可能遇到某个对自己结果非常清楚的人。你知道这一点。你就不需要花时间去问他们这方面的问题。也许你只想真正深挖：他们卡在哪里？一旦他们开始讲自己的现实和卡点，他们就会意识到，哦，我卡住是因为我的跨职能合作伙伴在挡我，而我和他们毫无关系基础。我其实需要去和他们见面，来一场突破性的对话，告诉他们我卡在哪了。所以有时候，把事情大声说出来，仅仅是给他们创造那个空间，就会对他们帮助巨大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's kind of an implication here that the person often knows the answer or can come to the answer, and they just need a little bit of nudge to get there.
turns.zh: 这里有一种隐含的意思：那个人往往知道答案，或者能自己得出答案，他们只是需要一点推动就能到达那里。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, this is definitely you want to coach when you think the person you're talking to has the right context and can solve their own problem. That's a premise of coaching. You wouldn't coach if someone needs your guidance and comes to you and says, "Hey, I'm trying to take my company public. You took your company public. Can you tell me exactly the steps you took to get there?" Not a good time to coach.
turns.zh: 对，这确实说明：当你认为交谈对象拥有正确的上下文、能解决自己的问题时，你才应该去 coaching。这是 coaching 的前提。如果有人需要你的指导，来找你说，"嘿，我想让公司上市。你让公司上市过。你能不能告诉我你具体是怎么做到的？"——那就不是 coaching 的好时机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This begs the question, what if they just come to a terrible conclusion and you're just like... Advice on when to actually just like, "What about this instead?"
turns.zh: 这就引出一个问题：如果他们得出了一个很糟糕的结论，而你只是……关于什么时候该真的说"那换成这个怎么样"，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, okay. I think that's great. So, if you have a really strong negative reaction to what they're sharing, of course it doesn't behoove anyone to hide that. I think you get curious. "Hey, help me understand how you came to that conclusion because here's my reaction to that." So, you're honest, but you're also curious. So, coaching in a manager or a leader context is not the same as in an executive coaching conversation. You're managing this person. You're responsible for their outcomes. You're not setting up an hour-long coaching session, you're just using coaching as an additional tool in your toolkit from advising. And you're creating more space, maybe 15% more space in your one-on-ones, in your meetings for open-ended questions.
turns.zh: 对，好。我觉得这问得很好。所以，如果你对他们分享的内容有非常强烈的负面反应，当然，藏着掖着对谁都没好处。我觉得你会带着好奇。"嘿，帮我理解一下你是怎么得出那个结论的，因为我对它有这样的反应。"所以，你既诚实，又保持好奇。所以，在经理或领导者的语境下做 coaching，和高管 coaching 对话不一样。你在管理这个人。你对他们的结果负责。你不是在安排一小时的 coaching 会话，你只是把 coaching 当作你"给建议"工具箱之外的一个补充工具。你是在创造更多空间，也许在你的 1对1、在你的会议里，多腾出 15% 的空间给开放式问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this phrase, help me understand. One of my managers used to be really good at this, just like... You could tell, he's like, "Help me understand this part of your thinking."
turns.zh: 我喜欢"帮我理解一下"这句话。我的一个经理以前就很擅长这个，就像……你能看出来，他会说，"帮我理解一下你这个思考的部分。"

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. And the other thing that does when you're curious and you don't just shut down someone's idea, is you're helping them think. You're not helping them realize they're going to screw it up unless they come to you for advice. You're helping equip them with the right questions to ask and the right skepticism to have. And so, it's always useful to be in conversation when someone who reports to you has a different worldview than you do. There's some reason they came up with this great idea that you think is a terrible idea. And actually, that's where the learning happens.
turns.zh: 对。而当你保持好奇、不立刻否定别人的想法时，另一件会发生的好事是：你在帮他们思考。你不是在帮他们意识到"除非来问你，否则他们会搞砸"。你是在帮他们装备上该问的正确问题，以及该有的正确质疑。所以，当你下属的世界观和你不同时，保持对话总是有用的。他们能想出这个你认为很糟糕的好点子，总有原因。而实际上，学习恰恰就发生在那里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you may actually be wrong and you may realize, okay, they actually have the better solution. I get it now.
turns.zh: 而且你可能其实是错的，你会意识到，好吧，他们其实有更好的方案。我现在懂了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. This actually happens to me all the time in talent conversations. Because I have a background in being an HR business partner, and I'm working with CEOs and they're thinking about building their leadership team. And I want everyone to have a very rigorous stance on their talent because if you have an A plus squad, you're going to do great things in the world. And sometimes, they come up with an idea to performance manage someone who's clearly not working in the role, but think, oh, maybe I'll wait six months, and then, we'll have a conversation. I have a strong point of view. I'm not going to let that slide, but I'm going to say, "Help me understand why that is a good idea," and I'm going to press on that. And if they don't come to an idea that I'm aligned with, I'm going to share openly my perspective while still empowering them to solve their own problem.
turns.zh: 对。这在我的人才讨论中其实一直都在发生。因为我有 HR 业务伙伴（HR business partner）的背景，我和 CEO 们合作，他们正思考如何搭建领导团队。我希望每个人对自己的人才都持非常严谨的立场，因为如果你有一支 A+ 战队，你就能在世界上成就大事。有时候，他们会对一个明显不胜任的人提出绩效管理方案，但又想，哦，也许我再等六个月，然后再谈。我有很强的主见。我不会让这事蒙混过去，但我会说，"帮我理解一下为什么这是个好主意"，然后我会追问。如果他们没能得出一个我认同的想法，我会坦然分享我的观点，同时仍然赋能他们去解决自己的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To close the loop on this piece of advice, is there an example you could share to make this super concrete for folks?
turns.zh: 为了让这个建议形成闭环，你能不能分享一个例子，让大家非常具体地理解？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Well, I'm going to give you an example of a client, I'm going to call him Jeff, who runs an AI company. And he was essentially playing the role of the head of product also. And he had a growing number of engineers and designers, and his customer base was growing rapidly. And he started to feel completely overwhelmed. So, he came to me and we started coaching together. And soon, he realized that he was the blocker on every decision, every business decision, every product decision. And he was resenting it. He wanted his team to take more ownership. But with some coaching, he realized he was training his team to come to him with every decision because he had always operated that way. So, he decided to create squads and have small pods of engineers, product leaders, and designers focus on subsets of the team. Very normal as you have a small startup scaling. But he didn't have an engineering manager and a product leader for every one of them. (00:26:00): So, this was a little bit earlier than he was equipped for because he did it out of necessity. And he also realized he needed to create some behavior change for the way he was interacting with that tech lead on each project so that they would take more ownership. So, we really invested in this idea of I'm going to start to set the system up so we have a product review every two weeks, they each have clear KPIs they're driving to that we co-design, and for this next quarter, I'm shifting from the role of deciding on everything to coaching. I'm going to really ask good questions in our check-ins. I'm going to align to the KPIs, ask how things are going, ask where they're stuck. And I just had a session with him last week. It's amazing to see him because he's so much more energized. He said, "The squads are moving so much faster. The teams feel more empowered and motivated." And he has time to pick his head up and plan for 2026...
turns.zh: 好，我给你讲一个客户的例子，我叫他 Jeff，他经营一家 AI 公司。而且他基本上也扮演着产品负责人的角色。他的工程师和设计师越来越多，客户群也在快速增长。他开始感到彻底不堪重负。于是他来找我，我们一起开始 coaching。很快，他意识到自己是每个决策、每个业务决策、每个产品决策的瓶颈。而他对此很怨恨。他想让团队承担更多 ownership。但通过一些 coaching，他意识到，正是因为自己一直都是那样运作的，他才在训练团队把每个决策都拿来找他。所以他决定组建小队（squads），让由工程师、产品负责人和设计师组成的小组分别聚焦团队的不同子集。这在小创业公司扩张时很正常。但他并没有给每个小队都配上工程经理和产品负责人。(00:26:00): 所以，这比他准备充分的时机稍微早了一点，因为他是在不得已之下才这么做的。而且他也意识到，他需要改变自己与每个项目技术负责人互动的方式，好让他们承担更多 ownership。所以，我们真正投入去落实这样一个想法：我要开始建立这套机制——每两周做一次产品评审，每个人有我们共同设计的、清晰要达成的 KPI，而在接下来的这个季度，我要从"决定一切"的角色转向 coaching。我要在我们的检查会上真正问出好问题。我会对齐 KPI，问进展如何，问他们卡在哪了。上周我刚和他做了一次会话。看到他真让人惊叹，因为他现在能量充沛多了。他说，"小队推进得快多了。团队感觉更有赋能、更有动力了。"而他也腾出了时间抬起头、为 2026 年做规划……

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And he has time to pick his head up and plan for 2026, and spend his time and his gifts. Which are product, vision and strategy. So that's more of a global example of what results from leaders shifting from the mode of solving every problem to coaching.
turns.zh: ……而且他腾出时间抬起头、为 2026 年做规划，把时间花在他的天赋上。也就是产品、愿景与战略。所以，这是一个更大层面的例子，展示领导者从"解决每个问题"的模式转向 coaching 会带来什么结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a great example of just the power of this, this makes your life so much better. Because other people can start picking up the slack and not come to you for everything. And it's like, listen better, ask a few powerful questions and so much improves, so much changes.
turns.zh: 这是一个太好的例子，展示了这件事的力量，它会让你的生活好太多。因为别人可以开始接手那些活儿，而不是什么都来找你。就像是，更好地倾听、问几个有力的问题，就会有那么多改善、那么多改变。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone around you gets better.
turns.zh: 你身边的每个人都变得更好。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Lenny, let's try it.
turns.zh: Lenny，我们来试一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's try it.
turns.zh: 好，我们来试一下。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: So I want you to tell me a challenge. It could be a personal challenge, a professional challenge. Just bottom line, something that you're struggling with.
turns.zh: 所以我想让你告诉我一个挑战。可以是个人方面的挑战，也可以是职业方面的。说白了，就是一件你正在挣扎、搞不定的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whoa. The main thing I struggle with these days is just endless work. I feel like this newsletter, I started this newsletter six, seven years ago at this point, and originally it was like, I'm just going to build this chill newsletter, do this on the side. Just kind of chill out for a while. And now it's just like, it just grows. I couldn't help but make it more awesome and bigger and have this podcast now and other stuff I got going on. So it's always this. (00:28:18): So I'm in a world now where it's just this ... the way I think about it is the Indiana Jones boulder is constantly in my back rearview mirror just coming at me. Because I need to get a newsletter post out, get podcast episodes out, do all the things associated with that. I'm also just in the middle of ... I have this large Slack community at Twitter and LinkedIn, so I'm just constantly being barraged with small little asks and things and all these little things that never ... it's hard to just ignore and say no to. So what I struggle with just endless work. I joke that be careful working for yourself if your boss is a workaholic.
turns.zh: 哇哦。我最近最大的困扰其实就是没完没了的工作。我感觉这个 newsletter，我是六七年前开始做的，最初就是，我就做一个轻松自在的 newsletter，当个副业。就先稍微躺平一阵子。而现在它就像，它自己在长大。我忍不住把它做得更厉害、更大，现在还有了这档播客，还有其他一堆我在弄的事。所以一直就是这样。(00:28:18): 所以我现在的世界就是……我把它想象成《夺宝奇兵》里那块巨石，一直在我的后视镜里朝我滚过来。因为我得把 newsletter 文章发出来，把播客节目录出来，做所有与之相关的事。而且我还处在……我在 Twitter 和 LinkedIn 上有个很大的 Slack 社群，所以我不断地被各种小小的请求和琐事轰炸，这些东西永远……很难直接无视、说"不"。所以我挣扎的就是没完没了的工作。我开玩笑说，如果你老板是个工作狂，那给自己打工要小心。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I totally relate to that. Okay, so I'm hearing noise, barrage of needs and just constant requests of you online, in your work life. There's always something that you need to be doing. And you designed it that way yourself. So you're kind of aware of, I had this one intention of a path to freedom, insight. I imagine the newsletter was a fun passion project. And you couldn't help but make it this all-consuming full-time job.
turns.zh: 我完全有同感。好，那我听到的是：噪音、各种需求的轰炸，以及线上和工作里对你的持续请求。总有事情需要你去做。而且这是你自己一手设计成的这个样子。所以你大概也意识到了，我原本是想走一条通往自由、洞见的路。我猜这个 newsletter 最初是个有趣的爱好项目。而你忍不住把它变成了这份吞噬一切的全职工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. Let me just add, it's like in so many ways the most awesome thing I could ever imagine doing also and extremely fulfilling. And I couldn't think of anything better I'd rather be doing.
turns.zh: 没错。让我补充一下，它在很多方面也是我能想象得到的最棒的事，而且极其有成就感。我想不出还有什么我更想做的事。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think that's an important element.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这是个重要的因素。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's this Indiana Jones boulder constantly chasing me.
turns.zh: 就是这块《夺宝奇兵》的巨石一直在追我。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, I can feel the gratitude and the resonance with what you get to do every day. And yet I hear you questioning, why does it have to feel like I'm fighting for my life while I'm doing this thing I love?
turns.zh: 对，我能感受到你对每天所做事的感恩和共鸣。然而我听到你在问，为什么在我做这件热爱的事时，它却感觉像是在为生存而战？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's one way to put it, yeah. This boulder is squishing me.
turns.zh: 可以这么说吧，是的。这块石头正在把我压扁。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I mean, the Indiana Jones boulder is coming for you.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，那块《夺宝奇兵》的巨石正在朝你过来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man.
turns.zh: 哦天。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That's a fight or flight instinct we all have.
turns.zh: 那是我们都有的"战斗或逃跑"本能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's true. That's true.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Okay, so thank you for being vulnerable enough to share that with your listeners and with me. I want to ask you, what would dream state look like? So let's say in six months you're still running this beautiful business that you've created. And you feel differently. What is happening?
turns.zh: 好，谢谢你这么坦诚地把它分享给你的听众和我。我想问你，理想的境地会是什么样？假设六个月后，你还在运营你创建的这家美好的公司。而你感觉不一样了。那时会发生什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I imagine is the same thing mostly, just much more free time. So more time to experiment and play with other things. And at the same time, the newsletter continues to be awesome and high quality, the podcast continues to be awesome and high quality. So it's continuing to put out the same high quality stuff, just more free time, less ... the boulders may be smaller.
turns.zh: 我想象的大致还是同一件事，只是有大量的空闲时间。也就是更多时间去尝试、去玩别的东西。同时，newsletter 继续保持出色和高质，播客也继续保持出色和高质。所以还是在输出同样高质量的内容，只是有更多空闲时间，少一点……石头可能会小一些。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, okay. So what does free time enable for you? When you think about ... I hear your deep commitment to quality products and quality output. But this longing to feel a little bit more playful or flexible with those parts that are essential to you.
turns.zh: 对，好。那么空闲时间能为你带来什么？当你想到……我听到你对高质量产品和高质量输出的深切投入。但你又渴望在那些对你至关重要的部分上，感觉更轻松、更灵活一些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very practically, it's time to play around with AI tools. Just explore and just kind of tinker. Versus, okay, all the time I have, I need to focus on the newsletter, make it better for next week. Oh, it's coming out, here's things I got to do. Oh, this podcast, got to prep for that, got to edit this thing. So it's just time to tinker and explore and just like that kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 很实际地说，就是去玩玩 AI 工具的时间。就是去探索、去捣鼓。而不是，好吧，我所有的时间都得聚焦在 newsletter 上，让它下周更好。哦，要发了，这些事我得做。哦，这个播客，得准备，得剪辑这个。所以就是去捣鼓、去探索的那种时间。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That makes sense. And what's important about exploring and tinkering to you?
turns.zh: 有道理。那么探索和捣鼓这件事，对你来说重要在哪里？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because in the work I do, I need to stay ahead on where things are going. I can't just sit around and pontificate from a cloud. I need to really understand how things work, what's working, what's not, what's real, what's not. So being on the ground as much as I can with what's actually going on versus just putting out content.
turns.zh: 因为在我做的工作里，我需要走在前沿、看清方向。我不能只是坐在云端空谈。我需要真正理解事情是怎么运作的，什么有效、什么无效，什么是真的、什么不是。所以要尽可能贴近实际发生的事，而不是只输出内容。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That makes sense. Your voice is moving really fast. I kind of hear you feeling behind, even in the way you're describing what you're doing.
turns.zh: 有道理。你语速变得很快。我有点听到你感觉落后了，甚至从你描述自己在做什么的方式里都能听出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A good [inaudible 00:32:09] listening.
turns.zh: 很好的 [inaudible 00:32:09] 倾听。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What's interesting to me is when you're talking about exploring and tinkering, when you first said it, you said it in kind of a spacious way. It's fun to explore and tinker. You're deeply naturally curious. You find new insights. But then I also heard you say, "And it's a way to stay ahead, I have to do it in order to feel like I'm informed." So what do you make of that difference?
turns.zh: 我觉得有意思的是，当你在说探索和捣鼓时，你第一次说的时候，语气里是有空间的。探索和多捣鼓很好玩。你天生就有深深的好奇心。你能发现新的洞察。但后来我也听到你说，"而且这是保持领先的方式，我必须做它才能觉得自己跟上了。"那么你怎么看待这个差别？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Those are two sides of the coin. There's another element of ... I guess let me answer that question. I think those are both true, I don't know. The reason I got into this is because it was so fun and so interesting. Just like, here's what's happening, here's what the future-
turns.zh: 对。对。这是一枚硬币的两面。还有另一个层面……我想我还是回答那个问题吧。我觉得这两面都是真的，我也不知道。我当初入这行是因为它太好玩、太有意思了。就像，这是正在发生的事，这是未来——

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here's advice, here's ways to improve in the work that you do. So I still love it. It's just I have less time to do that part and more it's just the machine of the treadmill of content, content, content. There's also just spending more ... I didn't even mention this. But just spending more time with my son and my wife, that would be really great just to have more freedom to go do stuff. Which we have a lot of that, but more is great.
turns.zh: 这是建议，这是改进你工作的方法。所以我依然热爱它。只是我做那部分的时间变少了，更多变成了内容、内容、内容这种跑步机的机器。还有花更多时间……我甚至没提到这个。但就是多花点时间陪我儿子和妻子，那会非常棒，多点自由去做别的事。我们现在已经有很多这样的时间了，但再多一点更好。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That makes sense. Okay, so the goal that I hear is not so dramatically different from today. It's that you hold on to this high quality output, but you have space for exploring and tinkering. And for spending quality time with the people you love most.
turns.zh: 有道理。好，那么我听到的目标，和今天并没有戏剧性的不同。就是你要守住这份高质量的输出，但你要有空间去探索和捣鼓。也要有空间去和你最爱的人共度高质量时光。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. One way I'm thinking about as you reflect that back is 25% more free time while everything else continues to be awesome. And the challenge I run into is I sometimes get that extra time and then I fill it with more projects and opportunities. That's the problem right there.
turns.zh: 对。当你把它反馈回来时，我想到的一种方式是：在其它一切依然出色的同时，多出 25% 的空闲时间。而我遇到的挑战是，我有时拿到了那点额外时间，然后又用它塞满了更多项目和机会。问题就在这里。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, there's that inertia of moving fast, taking advantage of the moment that's coming.
turns.zh: 对，就是那种快速运转的惯性，想要抓住即将到来的每一个时机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: So that's a perfect shift into, what are your current ways of operating that get in the way of having that 25% of free time?
turns.zh: 所以这就很自然地过渡到：你目前有哪些行事方式，挡住了你拥有那 25% 空闲时间的路？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's just agreeing to more things. Just like, oh look, I'm kind of free right now. Oh, okay, let's do this talk here. Let's agree to this thing here. So it's just once I feel freedom, I'm like, "Okay, I could do that other thing." And so I commit to more stuff.
turns.zh: 就是答应更多的事。就像，哦看，我现在有点空。哦好，那我们在这做个分享吧。我们答应这事吧。所以就是，一旦我感觉到了自由，我就会想，"好，我可以做那件别的事。"于是我就承诺了更多东西。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. And how is that commitment to saying yes to things that come at you serving you?
turns.zh: 对。那么这种对找上门的事说"好"的承诺，是在怎样地服务于你呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not great.
turns.zh: 不怎么样。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Well, it's serving you in some ways. You're doing it for a reason.

turns.en: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What benefit does it have to you?
turns.zh: 它对你有什么好处？

turns.en: Well, it depends on the thing. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。正是。

turns.en: Okay. So you're stuck in this kind of addiction to doing more and signing up for more, which is so normal in our world, and probably most listeners can relate to that. turns.zh: 好。所以你陷入了某种"做更多、接更多"的上瘾里，这在我们这个世界里太正常了，可能大多数听众都能感同身受。那是我们游其中的那锅"汤"。所以我们必须对我们周围的输入保持觉察。(00:35:34): 那么我们来探索你面前有哪些不同的选项。你提到你已经试过的一个，是列一张你不想再做的事、也就是你想说"不"的事的清单。并且真正承诺、坚持下去。还有别的什么做法，能帮你排定优先级，为你自己创造出那神圣的 25% 额外时间？

turns.zh: 我已经做过的一件事，虽然还没完全见效，但我真的很兴奋，就是我降低了 newsletter 和播客的发布频率。理论上，这应该是巨大的改变。但播客的频率还没降下来，要明年才会。newsletter 的频率，我基本上改变了给读者的承诺——不再是"你每周会收到一封 newsletter"，现在是"每月两到四次，看当时情况"。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which felt huge. The problem is I still like every week I'm like, "Oh, I want to write about this thing. Oh, every week there's nothing's happening, I got to put this out." turns.zh: 这感觉很大。问题是，我每周还是像，"哦，我想写写这个。哦，每周好像也没发生什么，我得把这发出来。"所以我几乎没利用好那个机会。所以我可以做的一件事，是干脆不要每周都发。(00:36:45): 另一件就是多找些帮手。这很难，因为已经有不少好帮手了，而别人能替我做的事就那么多，写一封出色的 newsletter、录这样的对话，别人是替不了的。但我一直在想，也应该更深入地想：哪里能让别人替我分担更多？

turns.en: Yeah, I love that insight. What I'm hearing is do less in certain areas and think about your team and really expanding the capacity of your team. turns.en: Just playing around with stuff. Just space to explore and tinker, and just sit around and think. Versus just go, go, go, go, go.

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. I just see you feel so light and excited in that. Like you almost are giddy when you think about that spaciousness.
turns.zh: 对。我都能看到你在那种状态里有多轻松、多兴奋。好像一想到那种开阔，你就几乎要乐疯了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That'd be so nice.
turns.zh: 那会太好了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And I just want to name reflect back to you how special that is and how much more creative you could be in your work when you have that space and time.
turns.zh: 而我只想点出来、反馈给你：那有多特别，以及当你有了那种空间和时间，你工作起来能有多么更有创造力。

turns.en: I love that.

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett

turns.en: I feel that, I feel that.

turns.en: I love that ... as we go through this, I'm thinking about this growth framework and I love how you're executing it. Like I see it in action, it's so good.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个……在我们走这个过程时，我在想这个成长框架，而我喜欢你执行它的方式。就像我亲眼看到它在运作，太好了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, I'm trying to do very simple coaching right now, just [inaudible 00:38:25]-
turns.zh: 对，我现在在尝试做非常简单的 coaching，只是 [inaudible 00:38:25]—

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. No, this is great
turns.zh: 对，对。不，这很棒

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: ... that it's really easy to follow for your listener.
turns.zh: ……就是它让你的听众真的很容易跟得上。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. This is great. Okay, so what's the one thing I could do in the next couple of weeks to help you move forward on this? turns.zh: 对，对。这很棒。好，那么未来几周里我能做的一件事是什么，能帮你在这方面往前推进？我觉得一个是至少跳过 newsletter 的一两周，真的坚持那个计划。但这很难，因为接下来两周我已经安排好了。我得写一个礼物指南，那是我的……好，那之后那周，我休息。好，酷。所以录这期节目的两周后，我不会发 newsletter。然后我要重新检视我对什么事说"好"、什么事说"不"的政策。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I love that. Think about everything you're saying yes to and what are things you want to say yes to that you could treat it with. So really consider that it's a trade off every time you say yes to something. The more resonant you are with the end state and what's possible for you, the easier it is to be disciplined in the near term.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。想想你对所有说"好"的事，以及你真正想说"好"的是什么——你可以带着这种心态去对待。所以要认真地意识到：每次你对某事说"好"，都是一种权衡取舍。你对自己最终状态和可能性的共鸣越强，短期里就越容易保持自律。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just that element of here's what you'll get out of this. It's not just no, no, no, no. It's like yes to this other thing you really, really want to do.
turns.zh: 我喜欢的就是这一点：这里是你从中能得到什么。不只是"不、不、不、不"。而是对那件你真的、真的想做的事说"好"。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. Exactly. Yes, say it like a resonant full body yes to the things that are in [inaudible 00:39:32].
turns.zh: 对。正是。对，要对那些在 [inaudible 00:39:32] 里的事，发出一种全身共鸣的"好"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hell yes.
turns.zh: 绝对的好（Hell yes）。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, hell yes. With an exclamation, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，hell yes。带着感叹号，正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.en: Well thank you, Lenny, for letting me just demonstrate what powerful questions are. And the reason I wanted to do that with you is you brought an example that's actually pretty big. But the same kinds of questions unlock new opportunity when it's about how to build technical infrastructure or how to influence the executive team or how to ship the go-to-market strategy. So I just want a name that's very transferable.
turns.zh: 嗯，谢谢你，Lenny，让我得以演示什么是有力提问。我之所以想和你做这个，是因为你带来的例子其实挺大的。它是一种情绪性的东西，是一种文化规范，是我们从小到大、尤其是在科技圈做事的过程中学会的一种存在方式。所以即便是这样的话题，用简单的 GROW 模型也会有用。但你的听众面对的话题往往非常复杂、技术性、且紧急。可是，当话题是关于如何搭建技术基础设施、如何影响高管团队、如何推出 go-to-market 策略时，同样那类问题也能解锁新的机会。所以我想强调的是，它非常具有可迁移性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that I got great advice in this conversation already.
turns.zh: 我喜欢的是，在这场对话里我已经得到了很棒的建议。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Good.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a great ROI for me at least.
turns.zh: 至少对我来说，ROI 太好了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What did it feel like to be coached on your own podcast?
turns.zh: 在自己的播客上被 coaching 是什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was unusual. I'm just like, wait, I got to get back to asking you questions. That's where our minds are right now.
turns.zh: 很不一样。我就是那种，等等，我得回到问你问题的状态。那才是我们现在心思所在的地方。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Okay, all right, all right. We can flip it, we can flip it. I do want to name that typically when you're coached versus told what to do, you're more bought in. So if I told you, Lenny, I've heard all kinds of leaders come to me talking about being too busy. Here's what you should do. Write a list of all the things you're doing, write the things you're going to delegate, cut out 25% of the things on your calendar. I could have given you a laundry list of things that I thought you should do without much context. But you're the expert on your own context and actually what resonates. And you're much more likely to do it if you came up with it.
turns.zh: 好，好，好。我们可以反过来，可以反过来。我确实想点出：通常当你被 coaching、而不是被告诉该怎么做时，你的认同感会更强。所以如果我告诉你，Lenny，我听过各种领导者来找我，说他们太忙了。这是你该做的。列一张你正在做的事的清单，写下你要委派出去的事，砍掉你日程上 25% 的事。我本可以在没有多少上下文的情况下，丢给你一长串我认为你该做的事。但你才是自己情境的专家，才知道什么真的能引起共鸣。如果是你自己想出来的，你更可能去做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to mention that earlier. That is so incredibly true. No one wants to ... unless you ask for advice, very few people are like, "Please tell me what to do."
turns.zh: 我刚才正想提这个。这太对了。没人想……除非你主动求建议，很少有人会说"请告诉我该怎么做"。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love just unsolicited advice. That doesn't go well.
turns.zh: 我真的很讨厌那种主动给的、没被请求的建议。那效果不好。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. And great leaders often say, "Do you want advice or do you want some space to think about it? Can I help you think it through? Or would you like me to tell you what I would do?" And both are fine in certain situations. So asking is useful too.
turns.zh: 对。而且优秀的领导者常常会问，"你想要建议，还是想要点空间自己想想？我能帮你把思路理清楚吗？还是你想让我告诉你我会怎么做？"而在某些情况下，两者都行。所以开口问也是有用的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. That's such an important element of this that we should have mentioned and I'm glad you did.
turns.zh: 对。好。这是这件事里很重要的一环，我们本该早点提的，我很高兴你提了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So I'm going to go back to asking you questions.
turns.zh: 好。那么我要回到问你问题的状态了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 太好了。

turns.en: This is a good segway to something I wanted to spend a little time on, which is burnout.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的过渡，引向我本来想花点时间聊的东西，也就是职业倦怠（burnout）。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm talking about is stuff that often leads to burnout. I'm definitely not burnt out, but this is a common problem in tech. Where people feel depleted and just go too hard. So many people I've worked with just left tech. I had a colleague at Airbnb, he's like a park ranger now near woods. That's how far tech-
turns.zh: 我说的这些东西，往往是导致 burnout 的原因。我绝对没有倦怠，但这是科技圈一个普遍的问题。人们感到被掏空，只是拼命往前冲。我合作过的好多人就这么离开了科技圈。我有个在 Airbnb 的同事，他现在在树林边当公园管理员。科技圈让人离开得有多远——

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: So peaceful.
turns.zh: 好宁静。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So peaceful and so wonderful. But I think that's just people go so hard sometimes and then just get burnt out and never want to do anything like this again. I know that you've spent a lot of time on this with founders and you have a really helpful approach. So just talk about what you've learned about helping leaders in tech avoid burnout and feel energized and excited about their work for a long time.
turns.zh: 那么宁静，那么美好。但我觉得，那只是有些人冲得太猛，然后就 burnout 了，再也不想做这类事了。我知道你在这方面和创始人花了大量时间，而且你有一套很有用的方法。所以就聊聊你在帮助科技圈领导者避免 burnout、并长期对工作保持干劲和热情方面学到了什么。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. Well first of all, I'm glad you brought it up. It's a huge problem. I remember when I was coaching top talent at Stripe, Patrick Collison is really committed to retaining top talent. And I created a program with my team for the top 50 executives in the tech side of the house. And we looked at their engagement scores, we did coaching circles. And it was so sad to see how exhausted that group of incredibly creative and committed leaders was in that moment. (00:43:19): And it's so common that people who start with incredible inspiration and incredible capacity start to feel like they've been pushing and pushing and pushing for years. They're parenting, they're leading, crazy things are happening to the business. And they just can't muster the same kind of motivation they once had. And I see this with my clients all the time. (00:43:44): So I've also witnessed people who are still inspired and continually energetic and seem to have some secret well of some diesel battery, or I guess I should say a Tesla battery that helps them through really hard challenges, and they're still having a good time. And so what I make of that is that when people are in their gifts and their strengths firmly, most of the time, they have more energy. We all have more energy when we're operating from the things we naturally are good at and the things we innately love doing. (00:44:25): So I try to help my leaders see that they can design their lives so they're spending 80% of their time in their gifts. That seems really ambitious because you're stuck within a context that requires a lot of you. Especially when you're executive at a huge company. But I also interact with founders who started a company with great inspiration, an entrepreneurial vision, and their job has obviously changed every six months. Once you fundraise, once you grow a team. And sometimes, especially technical founders will start solving a technical problem they're absolutely obsessed with. They spend three years doing it, the product ships, and then they're stuck managing a board and a team. And they don't even realize they're doing a completely different job than the one that played to their strengths. (00:45:17): So one tool I like to give is for people to actually take two weeks and every night reflect on, what are the five things today that gave me the most energy? And what are the five things that depleted my energy the most? If you do that for two weeks and you look at patterns, you can tell, what are the natural gifts that I'm living in? And what are the things that I'm stuck doing that are exhausting? And they're just slowly ... it's like a slow leak in your gas tank that over time shows up in your daily amount of energy.
turns.zh: 对。首先，我很高兴你提起来。这是个巨大的问题。我记得我在 Stripe 辅导顶尖人才时，Patrick Collison 对留住顶尖人才非常上心。我和我的团队为技术线 top 50 的高管做了一个项目。我们看了他们的敬业度分数，做了 coaching circle（教练圈）。看到那群极有创造力、极投入的领导者当时有多么疲惫，真的很让人难过。(00:43:19): 而那些带着惊人灵感和惊人能力起步的人，开始觉得自己几年来一直在推、推、推，这种情况太常见了。他们在育儿、在领导，业务上发生着疯狂的事。而他们就是鼓不起曾经有过的那种动力。我的客户里一直都有这种情况。(00:43:44): 但我也见过有些人依然受到启发、持续有能量，似乎有个秘密的"井"，装着某种柴油电池——或者我该说特斯拉电池——帮他们熬过真正艰难的挑战，而且他们依然乐在其中。所以我的理解是：当人们在绝大多数时间里稳固地处在自己的天赋和优势中时，他们会有更多能量。当我们做自己天生擅长、天生热爱的事时，我们都会更有能量。(00:44:25): 所以我试着帮我的领导者看到，他们可以设计自己的生活，让自己 80% 的时间都处在天赋区。这看起来很有野心，因为你被困在一个对你要求很高的语境里。尤其是当你是一家大公司的高管时。但我也和创始人合作，他们带着伟大的灵感和创业愿景创办公司，而他们的工作显然每六个月就变一次。一旦你融资了，一旦你组建了团队。而有时候，尤其是技术型创始人，会开始去解决一个他们极度痴迷的技术问题。他们会花三个……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I so believe this advice is so effective. This is the way I actually approach when I left my job. I very actively did this. I paid attention every day, what gave me energy? And what sapped my energy? And let me just do more of the thing that gave me energy and less of the thing that saps me. I want to talk about just like, there's only so much you can change, but I want to talk about that. And so initially I was like, maybe I'll become an advisor and consultant kind of person. I actually found that was super depleting for me.
turns.zh: 我太相信这个建议有多管用了。这其实是我离职时采用的方法。我非常主动地做了这件事。我每天留意，什么给了我能量？什么消耗了我的能量？然后我就多做给我能量的事，少做消耗我的事。我想说的是，你能改变的就那么多，但我想聊这个。所以一开始我以为，也许我可以当个顾问、咨询师之类的人。结果我发现那对我来说是极度消耗的。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Doing these calls and talking to people because it's like surface level, here are some things I would do. And it was just so unexciting and energizing. But writing was really energizing, which I'd never expected.
turns.zh: 做这些电话、和人们聊天，因为那就像浮于表面，"这是我会做的一些事"。而那太没劲了，也不提神。但写东西真的很提神，这是我从未预料到的。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's what I did, and I just followed that pole.
turns.zh: 而我就是那么做的，我只是顺着那根杆子走。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And it sounds like maybe you need a refresh, Lenny.
turns.zh: 而且听起来，也许你需要一次重新校准，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, interesting.
turns.zh: 哦，有意思。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: There's always more tuning you can do to your gifts. You're in this amazing ... you've clearly been successful for a reason, you're in your strengths and you're paying attention to what brings you energy. We can always do that more throughout our life. I think it's a process of continually tuning in to where your spark is. And protecting that spark, feeding it.
turns.zh: 对于你的天赋，永远还有更多可以调校的空间。你处在这个了不起的……你显然因为某种原因成功了，你处在自己的优势里，也在留意什么给你能量。我们一生都可以做得更多。我认为这是一个持续调频、找到自己火花所在的过程。并且保护那火花、喂养它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that insight, that just blew my mind. (00:47:08): So very tactically, the way you would do this is for two weeks every night is the idea, reflect back on that day and write down five things that gave you energy, five things that sap you of energy.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个洞察，简直让我醍醐灌顶。(00:47:08): 所以非常实操地说，做法是这样：连续两周，每天晚上回顾这一天，写下五件给了你能量的事、五件消耗了你能量的事。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, there's so many different activities you could use. So that's one. I like an activity of actually asking five to ten people in your life with a very simple email. When I walk in the room, what shows up? What are my strengths? What are the gifts? If you really don't know them and you haven't spent a lot of time in this realm, that's also an opportunity of actually asking the people who know you best, what your core gifts are? And when do you have the most inspiration? (00:47:46): You can also look through your calendar and note themes. Okay, over the last month, what are all the things I look at on my calendar that I'm excited to do? What are the things I dread? Okay, why do I dread those things? What do those things have in common? So there's various ways you can get to what is your zone of genius? But what my invitation is to take that really seriously. It actually takes risk taking, it takes intention to design your life around your gifts.
turns.zh: 对，你可以用很多不同的活动。所以那是一种。我喜欢的一个活动是，真的用一封很简单的邮件，去问你生命里五到十个人：当我走进房间时，你看到的是什么？我的优势是什么？我的天赋是什么？如果你真的不知道、也没在这方面花过多少时间，那其实也是一个机会——去问最了解你的人，你的核心天赋是什么？你什么时候最有灵感？(00:47:46): 你也可以翻看你的日历，找出规律。好，过去一个月里，我在日历上看到哪些事是让我兴奋去做的？哪些是让我害怕的？好，我为什么害怕那些事？那些事有什么共同点？所以有各种方法能让你找到自己的"天才区"（zone of genius）。但我邀请你的是，要认真对待这件事。围绕你的天赋去设计生活，其实需要冒险，也需要用心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any advice for actually doing this? Say someone's just like, "Yeah, I got to do this." But most people don't actually do this. Is there a buddy you can nominate, just help you do this? Is it like if you have an EA, they can maybe help you with this? Is there anything you've seen?
turns.zh: 关于真正去做这件事，有没有什么建议？假设有人就说，"对，我得做这个。"但大多数人其实不会真的去做。你能不能指定一个伙伴，帮你做这件事？比如如果你有 EA（行政助理），他们也许能帮你？你见过什么办法吗？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That's a good question. Yeah, I love your ideas. I think that the people around you need to be on board and know what are your gifts. So for example, when I was an HR business partner, my boss bought into this and I explained to her, "Hey, I started at Stripe because I actually know I'm going to be a coach. I'm not going to be Head of HR. But I love working with leaders. So I'm going to do all the compensation strategy and all the org design, and I'm going to help product and engineering leaders. But what I have in the back of my mind is I'm honing my coaching skills." (00:48:56): And so when this opportunity to work on top talent retention came about, it was very aligned in the realm of coaching and L&D, background that I had. So she put me on that. So it's useful to name it to the people around you. What are your gifts? What are your interests? What skills are you really excited to hone? So that they are in a contract with you to help you and really apply your gifts to the business's needs. So that's one thing. (00:49:23): When you're a founder, a CEO, when you have the autonomy to consider, what are the role scopes around me? Then you can really hire around it. So I have some CEOs that I work with who are incredible visionaries, great strategists, really good at managing the board, hiring, et cetera. Terrible at managing their team. They hate it. So they hire a COO. And they work in partnership, they have one person who's really internally focused, they get to be externally focused. That works well, it's a symbiotic relationship. If you're honest about your strengths and you're weaknesses, then you can start to manage around them.
turns.zh: 好问题。对，我喜欢你的想法。我认为你身边的人需要站在同一阵线，并且知道你的天赋是什么。举个例子，当我还是 HR business partner 时，我的老板接受了这个理念，我向她解释，"嘿，我来 Stripe 是因为我其实知道我将来要当教练。我不会当 HR 负责人。但我喜欢和领导者共事。所以我会做所有的薪酬策略、所有的组织设计，我会去帮产品和工程的领导者。但我心里想的是，我在打磨我的 coaching 技能。"(00:48:56): 所以当这个做顶尖人才保留的机会出现时，它和我 coaching、L&D（学习与发展）的背景非常契合。于是她让我去做那个。所以，把你的情况告诉身边的人是有用的。你的天赋是什么？你的兴趣是什么？你真正想打磨的技能是什么？这样他们就和你达成了一种默契，来帮你、并把你的天赋真正用到业务需求上。这是其一。(00:49:23): 当你是创始人、CEO，当你有自主权去思考"我周围有哪些角色范围"时，你就可以真正围绕它来招人。所以我有几个合作的 CEO，他们是了不起的远见者、出色的战略家，非常擅长管理董事会、招聘等等。但管理团队很糟糕。他们讨厌这个。于是他们招了个 COO。他们以伙伴关系合作，一个人真正对内聚焦，另一个人可以对外聚焦。这运作得很好，是一种共生关系。如果你对自己的优势和劣势诚实，你就能开始围绕它们来管理。
