turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is kind of an implied piece of this.
turns.zh: 这算是这件事里一个隐含的部分。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, I think sometimes people hire a Chief of Staff to help them and compliment them. Sometimes people design their team with strengths and gifts that they don't have. So it's really ... you can get creative once you really understand, oh, these things give me a ton of energy and these things are exhausting. But I still need to fill this need for the business. What are all the ways I can do it?
turns.zh: 对，我觉得有时候人们会招一个 Chief of Staff（幕僚长）来帮自己、补足自己。有时候人们会按自己不具备的优势和天赋来设计团队。所以真的……一旦你真正理解"哦，这些事给我大量能量、那些事让我筋疲力尽"，你就可以发挥创意了。但我依然需要为业务填补这个需求。我有哪些办法可以做到？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And telling your manager, I think, is such a simple and important part of this. Telling them-
turns.zh: 而告诉你的经理，我认为，是这件事里如此简单又重要的一环。告诉他们——

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... here's where I want to go, here's the things I want to get better at, here's the things that give me energy. Can we just try to make as much of my role that?
turns.zh: ……这是我想要去的方向，这是我想变得更好的事，这些是给我能量的事。我们能不能尽量让我的角色往这方面靠？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. Especially if you're executing well, people want to retain you. They want to know, what's going to keep you here for the next five years? And typically they think that means moving up the ladder. But maybe it doesn't for you. I think it does take the courage to move horizontally sometimes to get into your strengths. I mean, I've moved horizontally a number of times and I love what I do, I feel like I'm in my natural gifts. But it took me a few risks and some uncomfortable jobs that didn't feel like they were worthy of my experience in order to get there.
turns.zh: 对。尤其是当你执行得很好时，人们想留住你。他们想知道，是什么能让你在这里待下五年？而通常他们认为那意味着往上爬。但对你来说也许不是。我认为，有时候确实需要勇气去横向移动，才能进入你的优势区。我的意思是，我横向移动过好几次，而我热爱我所做的事，我感觉自己处在天生的天赋里。但要达到那里，我冒过几次险，也做过一些配不上我资历、让我不舒服的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a good percentage of your work life that should be in gifts and things that energize you versus, okay, I actually got [inaudible 00:52:48] stuff.
turns.zh: 你的工作生活里，有多少比例应该花在天赋和让你提神的事上，相对地，好吧，我其实还有 [inaudible 00:52:48] 那些事。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: My litmus test is 80%, that's the goal.
turns.zh: 我的检验标准是 80%，那是目标。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That's the aspiration. You're always going to have 20% of things you don't love doing. There's just the logistics of getting into the zone that you need to be in. But I really try to push people to think aspirationally, that if you're 80% of the time in your gifts, how much energy you have to give to the world. It's so much more inspiring. (00:53:09): So I want to tell you why I'm passionate about this topic because it actually is how I ended up as an Executive Coach. So 10 years ago, I was working at a small company called Remind, and I was running the UX Research team. And the CEO asked me to move into the Product Manager role for the Core Product team. And I was excited for the opportunity. I had non-technical background, but I thought, "Hey, all these strategists are up there creating the roadmap. I can do that. I know exactly what our users need." So I was excited for this. (00:53:44): I came into the team, there was I think 12 senior engineers, very opinionated, very skeptical, this non-technical PM, but we worked together. And what I did was I listened. I learned what do our users need? What does this team need? What's working and not working? And with-
turns.zh: 那是抱负。你永远会有 20% 的事是你不爱做的。只是为了进入你该待的那个状态，总有些后勤杂事。但我真的会推着人们去怀抱抱负地想：如果你 80% 的时间都在天赋里，你能给世界多少能量。那要鼓舞人得多。(00:53:09): 所以我想告诉你我为什么对这话题这么有热情，因为这其实是我最终成为高管教练的原因。十年前，我在一家叫 Remind 的小公司工作，我领导着 UX 研究团队。CEO 让我转到核心产品团队的 PM（产品经理）岗位。我对这个机会感到兴奋。我背景不是技术出身，但我想，"嘿，那些战略家在上面制定路线图。我能做。我清楚我们的用户需要什么。"所以我很兴奋。(00:53:44): 我进了团队，我记得有 12 个资深工程师，很有主见、很怀疑这个非技术背景的 PM，但我们一起共事了。而我做的事就是倾听。我了解到我们的用户需要什么？这个团队需要什么？什么在起作用、什么没起作用？然后——

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What does this team need? What's working and not working? And within a month, this team was working well together. They were reviewing each other's code base. They were really disagreeing in a healthy way in our team meetings. They felt more connected to users. And I felt like, "Okay, this rhythm is working." But what I was also doing as I was at home stressing in the middle of the night about the new user experience, I couldn't decide which of the designs to go with. I was always over leveraging our data scientists, and I found myself swirling on decisions that didn't need to have so much stress involved. And one day I went for a walk with my colleague Zach Abrams, and he was a great product manager and he was listening to me ask all these questions about how to sell the vision of what this product would look like in the future. (00:54:55): And he said, "Rachel, you're a zone of genius or your gift is not being a product strategist, but I've watched you over the last few months, and you have gotten the team more motivated than I ever could, and you've influenced the entire executive team behind your ideas, and that's impressive. You're a people person." And at first I was offended. What? You think I don't have the ability to be a great product leader? And yet I sat with what he said, and I knew he was right. Both my parents are therapists. I never wanted to be a therapist. Here I am. I'm basically a work therapist. I love entrepreneurial energy, I love big vision, but I'm a people person. (00:55:40): And I left that, and I realized I love what my coach does. I got trained as a coach. I went into HR leadership. And Zach, who was a gifted product strategist, went on to lead product at Coinbase and BREX and most recently Bridge, which was acquired by Stripe, and he's still my client. And we've watched our journeys over the last decade, and we've both been honing our gifts. Life is more fun when you're in your gifts, and you have more inspiration and capacity to offer the world. So I just want to share that story because it's helpful to be honest with the people you care about when they seem energized and when they seem depleted because sometimes it's a wakeup call for people to really think about what is their spark and to protect it and to feed it.
turns.zh: 这个团队需要什么？什么在起作用、什么没起作用？一个月内，这个团队就协作得很好了。他们互相审阅代码库。在团队会议里，他们会真正地、健康地各执己见。他们觉得自己和用户更连接了。而我当时觉得，"好，这个节奏是有效的。"但我同时在做的另一件事是：深夜在家为新用户体验焦虑，我没法决定选哪个设计。我总是过度依赖我们的数据科学家，并发现自己在一些本不需要那么多压力的决定上打转。有一天我和同事 Zach Abrams 去散步，他是个很棒的产品经理，他听着我问所有那些关于"如何兜售这个产品未来长什么样"的问题。(00:54:55): 他说，"Rachel，你的天才区、你的天赋不是当产品战略家，而是我过去几个月观察你，你让团队的积极性比我所能做到的都高，你让你的想法影响了整个高管团队，这很了不起。你是个擅长与人打交道的人（people person）。"一开始我很不爽。什么？你觉得我没有能力成为一个伟大的产品领导者？但我坐下来消化了他的话，我知道他是对的。我的父母都是治疗师。我从不想当治疗师。结果我成了。我基本上是个"工作治疗师"。我热爱创业能量，热爱宏大愿景，但我是个擅长与人打交道的人。(00:55:40): 我离开了那个岗位，意识到我热爱我的教练所做的。我接受了教练培训。我进入了 HR 领导层。而 Zach，那个有天赋的产品战略家，后来去了 Coinbase 和 BREX 领导产品，最近又去了 Bridge（被 Stripe 收购），他至今还是我的客户。过去十年我们看着彼此的旅程，我们都在打磨自己的天赋。当你处在天赋里，生活更有趣，你也有更多灵感和能……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that story because I think most people when they hear this advice and this topic of, "Okay, I am feeling depleted, I'm feeling burnt out," I feel like most people jump to, "Okay, but I can't actually do anything about it. I have a job. I got responsibilities." What I'm getting from this is the most important step is jump to figure out what you actually should be doing. What gives you energy? What your gifts are. It feels like that's the biggest gap for people because once you know that, there are ways to do that. Talk to your manager. "It may not be possible today, but here's where I want to be going. Here's what I want to be spending time on." I love your point you made though about you actually have to be doing well for your manager to listen to you. You can't just be sucking and then like, "Oh, but I want to work on strategy."
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个故事，因为我觉得大多数人听到这个建议、听到"好吧，我感到被掏空、我感到 burnout"这个话题时，都会跳到，"好吧，但我其实对此做不了什么。我有工作。我有责任。"我从中学到的是，最重要的一步是跳过去弄清楚你真正应该做什么。什么给了你能量？你的天赋是什么？这似乎是人们最大的缺口，因为一旦你知道了，就有办法去做。和你的经理谈。"也许今天还不行，但这是我想去的方向。这是我想花时间做的事。"不过我喜欢你提的那一点：你其实得表现得好，经理才会听你的。你不能自己一团糟，然后说，"哦，但我想做战略。"

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. Well, it's no one else's job to help you live in your gifts. And what I notice in big companies is people are often annoyed or frustrated with their management for not making their job more interesting. It's like, "No, your manager's job is to help you perform in the job you were hired to do. It's your job to navigate your career." So over the arc of your career, how do you match your gifts with the world's needs? And if the world right now is your company, how do you understand the needs enough so that you can apply your strengths to those needs?
turns.zh: 对。嗯，没人有义务帮你活在自己的天赋里。我在大公司观察到，人们常常对管理层感到恼火或沮丧，因为管理层没让工作变得更有趣。就像，"不，你经理的职责是帮你在被聘来做的那份工作上表现出色。经营你的职业生涯是你自己的事。"所以在你整个职业生涯的弧线里，你怎么让你的天赋与世界的需求匹配？而如果此刻的世界就是你的公司，你怎么充分理解那些需求，好把你的优势用上去？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me, there's a couple of guests I've had on the podcast who did this. They're both founders, so this is specific to founders, but Rahul Vohra at Superhuman, he realized he's not the best executor operations person, so he hired a president that took all that office plate. And then Darmesh, co-founder of HubSpot, he knew from the beginning he didn't want to manage people, so he made a rule with his co-founder, "I will never have reports." And he's the CTO, I believe, and has zero reports, has no one-on-ones.
turns.zh: 这让我想起，我播客上请过几位这样做的嘉宾。他们都是创始人，所以这针对的是创始人，但 Superhuman 的 Rahul Vohra，他意识到自己不是最好的执行运营的人，所以招了个总裁把那堆办公室的活儿都接了。还有 HubSpot 的联合创始人 Darmesh，他从一开始就知道不想管人，所以和联合创始人定了个规矩，"我永远不会有下属。"我相信他是 CTO，零下属，没有一对一面谈。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. And I think that it's a beautiful thing to recognize that, but then to actually address the needs of those reports also. I think often people know, "Ugh, I don't want to have one-on-ones," but just not having anyone to manage those people is not going to be healthy for your company. So you have to both take your strength seriously and actively manage around your weaknesses.
turns.zh: 对。而且我认为，认识到这一点很美好，但接着也要真正去满足那些"下属"的需求。我觉得人们常常知道，"哎，我不想做一对一面谈，"但光是不安排任何人去管理那些人，对你的公司不会健康。所以你既要认真对待自己的优势，也要主动围绕自己的劣势来管理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any maybe last piece of advice on this topic of helping people get to a place where they're feeling much less depleted and just more energized at work?
turns.zh: 关于帮助人们达到"没那么被掏空、在工作中更有能量"这个状态，有没有也许是最后一条建议？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I would start small. You don't have to leave your job and redesign your life. You can stop going to the optional things that are exhausting. You can leave space between the things that are depleting that you have to go to outside and go on a 30-minute walk and refuel your tank. Start with tomorrow. What are the three things you're going to do to plug up that gas leak and re-energize your spark? It might even be you love to read and you're going to start reading 30 minutes before you go to sleep every night. It doesn't have to be a dramatic life change, but recognize that only you know what is resonant and what is depleting, and it's your job to take that seriously if you want to show up purposeful and impactful in the world.
turns.zh: 我会从小处着手。你不必离职、重新设计人生。你可以不去参加那些可选的、让人筋疲力尽的事。在那些你必须去的、消耗性的事之间，你可以留出空间，去外面散个 30 分钟的步，给油箱加满油。从明天开始。你要做哪三件事来堵住那个漏油的地方、重新点燃你的火花？甚至可能是你爱读书，你打算每晚睡前读 30 分钟。这不必是戏剧性的人生改变，但要认识到：只有你知道什么与你共鸣、什么在消耗你，而如果你想在这个世界上目标明确地、有影响力地出现，认真对待这件事就是你的责任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. I've actually started reading before bed for 30 minutes, and that's been so joyful, like a physical book with a little nightlight.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个建议。我其实已经开始睡前读 30 分钟书了，那真是太愉悦了，就像拿个小夜灯配一本实体书。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I agree. I love a physical book. I have a Kindle, I got all the things, but a physical book on the couch is the best.
turns.zh: 我同意。我热爱实体书。我有 Kindle，该有的都有，但沙发上的一本实体书是最好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's just that nightlight is key because sometimes at nighttime you need a night book. So we've been talking mostly so far about individual improvement, how to figure out what you should be working on, just helping learning to coach, things like that. I want to take us up a little level above and talk about team skills, how people get better at working with other people. Something that you are in many ways known for is helping co-founders build better relationships. And in my experience one of the most challenging parts of starting a company is the co-founder relationship. A lot of people don't realize what they're getting into. You're basically getting married to this person in a very high stress situation, and you sometimes don't know much about them.
turns.zh: 对，关键就是那个小夜灯，因为有时候晚上你需要一本"夜间书"。所以我们到目前为止主要聊的是个人提升，怎么搞清楚你该做什么、怎么学 coaching，类似这些。我想把层级往上提一点，聊聊团队技能，人们怎么更好地和别人共事。你在很多方面以帮联合创始人建立更好的关系而闻名。而在我的经验里，创业最具挑战性的部分之一就是联合创始人关系。很多人没意识到自己卷入了什么。你基本上是在一种压力极大的情况下和这个人"结婚"，而且你有时对他们并不了解。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you not working well together is just a huge issue because that all trickles down, and everyone sees it. And when co-founders leave, it's really bad for everyone. So let me just ask you this, what have you found most helpful in helping co-founders build great relationships, stay happy and productive?
turns.zh: 而你们配合不好，就是个巨大的问题，因为这会层层往下渗，每个人都看在眼里。而联合创始人离开时，对所有人都是重创。那么我就问你这个：在帮助联合创始人建立好的关系、保持快乐和高效方面，你发现什么最有帮助？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, thanks for asking this. I love working with co-founders because I think your core values as a person come out when they interact with someone else's core values. Conflict, healthy conflict or otherwise, is actually where your core values come out. So it's fascinating to watch people try to do something incredibly hard in the context of someone else's vision, someone else's strengths and weaknesses and navigate that together. So there's so much energy in the co-founder dynamic for me and for co-founders themselves. It's actually something that people don't feel comfortable going to their board about or talking to that many people about because it's a private matter. It's almost like in a marriage you go see a couples' therapist, but you don't tell all your friends that you can't stand your partner, but it keeps you up at night. So it's a really tender, important relationship, and there aren't enough supports for co-founders to navigate it. It's very normal. (01:01:50): In fact, I know you probably know this stat, 65% of startups fail because of co-founder conflict, and co-founders are in a moment where they're trying to build the future for their business, but also trying to build their own livelihood. So there's so much at stake to get along with your co-founder. I think the core at its core, what you need in a healthy relationship is, one, self-awareness. What do I bring into this dynamic, and how am I being experienced by the other person? What does this other person bring into the dynamic, and how am I reacting to that? So the first is just collective awareness about what is our dynamic. I like to use the Enneagram for this, but there's all kinds of tools, self-awareness tools that you can use to give a common language to what is my thing and what is your thing. (01:02:46): A very classic one has to do with roles. CTOs tend to be skeptics. They love facts, they seek knowledge. They want depth of awareness and understanding, and they also like to be self-sufficient. This is a total generalization, but I've seen this pattern over and over again. The CEO is the person who had to sell the vision. They're a person who loves big picture vision strategy. They often are great at influencing others. They love to sell ahead of the reality of what the company's actually built. This creates an inherent tension between blind optimism and skepticism, and it's a dance that these two roles play together. So the first part is knowing the dance you're in, so you're not just stepping on each other's toes blindly. (01:03:34): The second step is actually being conscious about the commitment you're making to your relationship. In a marriage, for example, I talk about co-founder vows and recommitments and renewals because in a marriage you get married, and a lot of times people build a family and then they think, "Oh, the relationship will just continue around each other all the time. We're doing this thing together." But just like couples need a date night, co-founders need time and space to connect with each other to come together and say, "How's this working for you? Are we still aligned on our vision and our strategy? How are we working together? What am I doing that's pissing you off? What are the things that have gone unsaid and that we need to talk about?" (01:04:20): But if you're just in the hustle and bustle of running and scaling your startup, you don't make time for that conversation. So I think it's incredibly important for co- founders to make space for their relationship, whether that's a dinner every other week, whether that's going out to lunch regularly, whether that's just touching base business-wise, but having an in-person quarterly check-in. That space is critical for the health of a co-founder relationship.
turns.zh: 对，谢谢你问这个。我热爱和联合创始人合作，因为我认为，当一个人的核心价值观与另一个人的核心价值观互动时，你自己的核心价值观就会显现出来。冲突，无论健康与否，其实正是你的核心价值观显现的地方。所以看着人们在别人的愿景、别人的优势与劣势的语境里，一起去尝试做一件极其困难的事，并共同应对，是非常迷人的。所以在联合创始人的互动里，无论对我还是对他们自己，都有巨大的能量。这其实是人们不愿向董事会提起、也不愿和太多人聊的事，因为那是私事。几乎就像在婚姻里你去看伴侣咨询，但你不会告诉所有朋友你受不了你的伴侣，可它让你夜不能寐。所以这是一种非常微妙、重要的关系，而能帮助联合创始人应对它的支持太少了。这很常见。(01:01:50): 事实上，我知道你可能知道这个数据：65% 的创业公司因为联合创始人冲突而失败，而联合创始人正处于既要为公司的未来打拼、又要为自己生计打拼的时刻。所以和联合创始人处好关系，利害关系太大了。我认为，一段健康关系的核心，第一是自我觉察。我给这段关系带来了什么？对方是怎么体验我的？对方给这段关系带来了什么？我又在如何回应？所以首先只是对"我们的互动模式是什么"达成共同的觉察。我喜欢用九型人格（Enneagram）来做这个，但各种自我觉察工具都可以，用来给我们的"东西"和"你的东西"提供一套共同语言。(01:02:46): 一个非常经典的和角色有关。CTO 往往是怀疑论者。他们热爱事实，追求知识。他们想要深度觉察和理解，而且他们也喜欢……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that second piece, the vows idea is such a good idea. Is that something you actually recommend, here's what I vow to do?
turns.zh: 关于那第二点，"誓约"的想法真是个好主意。这真是你实际会建议的——"这是我誓要做的事"？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, here's what I commit to do. So recently I actually wrote an article with First Round, and we created a document to help co-founders think about what to integrate into their check-in. So we put out weekly check-in, monthly check-in and annual and just questions to sit down and ask each other. Active listening skills will come in handy in those conversations, but it's about taking space out of hustling and running the business to think about the business from a like to say, instead of being on the dance floor, you need time on the balcony to look down at what's happening. How are we doing? Is this still working for both of us? And the vows are really about, how are we going to be together? How are we going to show up? What's our culture that we're creating? (01:05:43): Even if you don't want to go through a whole culture exercise early on in building your company, you should have some sense of how you want to show up for each other. How are we going to make decisions? How are we going to deal with conflict? These are things you can go into intentionally and design with your co-founder.
turns.zh: 对，这是"我承诺要做的事"。所以最近我其实和 First Round 合写了一篇文章，我们做了一个文档，帮联合创始人思考该把什么融入他们的定期对齐（check-in）里。我们给出了周对齐、月对齐和年度对齐，以及坐下来互相问的问题。积极倾听的技巧在这些对话里会派上用场，但关键是从"拼命经营业务"中抽出身来，退一步思考业务——就像说，与其在舞池里，你需要到阳台上去俯瞰正在发生什么。我们做得怎么样？这对我们俩还有效吗？而誓约真正关乎的是：我们要怎么在一起？我们要怎么出现？我们在创造一种什么样的文化？(01:05:43): 即便你不想在公司早期做整套文化梳理，你也应该对"你想怎么为彼此出现"有点感觉。我们要怎么做决策？我们要怎么处理冲突？这些是你可以有意地、和你的联合创始人一起设计的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to link to that post The first step, Enneagram sounds like that's what you recommend, and this is basically a personality profile that a lot of people love.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会附上那篇文章的链接。第一步，九型人格听起来就是你推荐的，而它基本就是一种很多人喜欢的性格画像。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I really like the Enneagram. I think you can also simply tell each other, "Here are my strengths. Here's what I see as my weaknesses, and what do you think? Give me some feedback. Do you agree?" And you can do that with each other without any personality assessment. If you want to just be scrappy and have an open connected conversation about, you could even say, what are the gifts I bring and the weaknesses I have, and how will I cover those? How will I lean into my gifts? How will I cover my weaknesses, and how will you? And then I think it's worthwhile having a conversation about, what are the gaps neither of us cover that we're likely going to need as we build this business?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢九型人格。但我认为你也可以简单地互相告诉对方，"这是我的优势。这是我认为我的劣势，你怎么看？给我点反馈。你同意吗？"你们不用做任何性格测试也能这么做。如果你想就事论事、来一场开放而连接有度的对话，你甚至可以说，我带来的天赋是什么、我有的劣势是什么，我要怎么补这些？我要怎么发挥我的天赋？我要怎么补我的劣势，你又要怎么补？然后我认为值得聊的是：在我们构建这门生意的过程中，有哪些缺口是我们俩都没覆盖、却很可能会需要的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you recommend people do when they are just like, "Our relationship isn't working great. There's a lot of tension"? All this advice we've been talking about, at the beginning, here's things you can do to set things up for success. Understand what you're good at, what you're bringing to the table. Consciously commit to, here's what I'm going to do, here's what you're going to do. Have these dinners or lunches. I love this metaphor of going out on the balcony and just reflecting on how it's going. So that's all really great. What if you're just already in it and it's really annoying, I don't like this person that much or so much tension constantly. What are a couple things they can do this week, next week?
turns.zh: 当人们就是像"我们的关系不太好。张力很大"时，你建议他们做什么？我们聊的这些建议，都是在开头——你可以做这些来为成功铺路。搞清楚你擅长什么、你能贡献什么。有意识地承诺：这是我要做的、这是你要做的。搞这些晚餐或午餐。我喜爱"走到阳台上去、反思一下进展如何"这个比喻。所以那一切都很棒。但如果你已经深陷其中、真的很烦，你不太喜欢这个人，或一直有这么大的张力呢？他们这周、下周能做哪几件事？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Co-founders typically come to me either in this early phase where they want to intentionally build something great and they want to set it up for success. More often co-founders come when they're really frustrated with one another. They feel the tension is palpable. They can't stand it anymore, but they're still really deeply committed to the business so they don't see an out. And they knew that at some point they really loved this cofounder, so they see a possibility of recovering, and that's why they want to go get a coach. I'm going to give you an example of this PR duo running a fierce business scaling really fast. And at one point when they started, you had the visionary who was great at selling business. They were both incredible with PR, and the partner was incredible operationally. (01:08:17): So as the business scaled, one took on a lot more business development and the other took on all the internal things, but was exhausted by all this people management and all of the elements of running a scaled team that she didn't expect to have to do. And when they came, I think both of them weren't sure, can we figure this out? Do we want to just sell this thing? Do we want to keep going? And I think someone said, "End it or send," was what one co-founder said to me. They're coming at this decision point. And what I saw them do is, one, they named current state really well. They were both able to share. We did use a 360. So they got feedback from their teams and then shared it with one another, but they were able to be open and vulnerable in what was working and what wasn't working. Not immediately, but over time. (01:09:16): And they realized they used to love being partners in this work, but as they began to lead different teams, they grew very distant from one another. They were living on opposite sides of the country and actually just coming together and realizing what each other was missing and how lonely it is to lead this scaling company without each other's support and how they actually needed the counterbalance to their strengths and didn't have it was a important start to their healing. (01:09:48): And over our coaching, they turned back towards each other and they created more of a rhythm of how they would get together without me involved. And they ended coaching after our arc feeling renewed and really recommitted. They made some changes on their leadership team to fill their gaps. They also started, I think, meeting once a week virtually, and they started a cadence of getting together in person quarterly. And I don't mean to say that just that time means you're going to heal, sometimes coming together and really grappling. I had one last week where we all came together, we had a great full day in-person discussion about how they were making this co-founder duo, how they were making decisions. (01:10:36): And after that conversation, it was really clear that one of the co-founders was unhappy and didn't appreciate the other one and was not going to change and realized he was a big part of the problem and I think is going to leave the business. But that's still success because it's clarity. You're not muddling in the dark, frustrated, unconscious about the interpersonal dynamics you're in, you're making a choice based on your strengths and what the business needs and this relationship dynamic that you're in to either be in it or to lovingly step out of it.
turns.zh: 联合创始人找我，通常要么是在早期阶段——他们想有意地建出伟大的东西、为成功铺路；更常见的是，他们在彼此真的很沮丧时来找我。他们感到张力清晰可感。他们再也受不了了，但他们依然对这门生意有很深的承诺，所以看不到出路。而他们知道，曾经有段时间他们真的很爱这个联合创始人，所以他们看到挽回的可能，这就是为什么他们想去找个教练。我给你举一个例子：这对做 PR 的二人组，经营着一门飞速扩张的猛业务。一开始，有个远见者很擅长谈生意。他们俩 PR 都极厉害，而那位搭档在运营上极厉害。(01:08:17): 所以随着业务扩张，一个承担了更多业务拓展，另一个承担了所有内部事务，但却被所有这些人员管理、以及运营一个规模化团队她没料到要做的元素累垮了。当他们来找我时，我觉得两人都不确定：我们能搞定吗？我们想直接卖掉吗？我们想继续吗？我记得有个人说，"要么结束、要么……"（end it or send），这是一位联合创始人跟我说的。他们正处在这个决策点上。而我看到他们做的第一件事，是把当下状态说得很清楚。两人都能分享。我们确实用了 360 度反馈。所以他们从团队那里得到反馈，然后彼此分享，但他们能在"什么在起作用、什么没起作用"上做到开放和坦诚。不是立刻，而是随着时间。(01:09:16): 他们意识到，他们曾经热爱做这项工作的搭档，但随着他们开始领导不同的团队，彼此变得非常疏远。他们住在国家的两端，而真的只是聚到一起，才意识到彼此缺了什么，以及在没有……的情况下领导这家扩张中的公司有多孤独[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how similar this is to just the marriage, all this stuff. This is the same sort of thing you would do.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这和婚姻多么相似，所有这些。这就是你会做的同一种事。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Totally. I mean a marriage, you're building a life with a partner. So the only difference is a marriage is rooted in sexual attraction and love, and that's not the case always in the co-founder dynamic. But I have worked with couples who are also co-founders, but there should be some element of love for your co-founder. In fact, I think that when you work closely with colleagues and you really are able to see their gifts and enable them, you can't help but love them.
turns.zh: 完全。我的意思是，婚姻里，你是在和伴侣共建人生。所以唯一的区别是，婚姻根植于性吸引和爱，而联合创始人的关系不总是这样。但我确实和既是夫妻又是联合创始人的人合作过，而对你的联合创始人，应该有某种爱的成分。事实上，我认为当你和同事紧密合作、并真正能看到他们的天赋、赋能他们时，你会忍不住爱上他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a big statement. The other takeaway here is that just get coaching. It feels like that's the solution if things are just not working great. There's only so far you can get just talking.
turns.zh: 这话分量很重。另一个收获就是：干脆去 coaching。感觉如果事情就是不太顺，那就是解决办法。光靠聊天，你能走的距离有限。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: It takes an evolved facilitator, one of the co-founders, being able to hold space for both their frustration and their empathy in a dynamic that is challenging. So outside support is useful. Sometimes it's actually a team member, it's an HR leader. It's the GC who happens to have great people skills. You don't always need a coach, but you need space to be vulnerable, open, and curious. So if you can create that on your own, that's great. I think it's definitely possible.
turns.zh: 这需要一个成熟的引导者——可以是联合创始人之一——能在充满挑战的互动里，既容纳他们的沮丧、也容纳他们的共情。所以外部支持是有用的。有时候其实是个团队成员、是个 HR 负责人。是那个碰巧很擅长人际的 GC（总法务）。你不一定总需要教练，但你需要一个可以坦诚、开放、好奇的空间。所以如果你能自己创造那个空间，那就很好。我认为这绝对是可能的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Outside of the co-founder relationship, do you have any just tactical tips for people to improve their interpersonal skills with just team members, anyone they work with, just people that may struggle like, "Man, I have a hard time with this person. I just have a hard time with a lot of people"?
turns.zh: 除了联合创始人关系，你有没有什么实操的小技巧，帮人们改善和团队成员、和任何共事者的关系——就是那些可能挣扎的人，"天，我和这人处不来。我就是和很多人处不来"？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: First of all, people when they want to have a conflict or they want to engage in something that's not working, they come in armored and ready to prove their point. It's natural. You've been thinking about this, perseverating over whether you should mention it. You finally get to the point of engaging, and often there's a misguided view that the goal is to convince the other person that what they're doing is wrong. Actually, the goal of any conflict is to create mutual understanding. So when I go in to have a conversation with, let's say my husband who's not doing his share of the parenting, my goal is to help him understand what I'm struggling with so that he can empathize, see clearly what's happening, and perhaps meet my needs in some way. But it's not for me to prove to him how little he's doing in the house because he might have a totally different story about what's happening. (01:13:54): So I'm going to give you a framework that I like that many of my clients use. It's from Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication. It is a book and a framework. So it's four steps. The first step is observations. So my job is to note what is happening factually. For example, I noticed that in the last three sprint planning meetings, you didn't invite me to those conversations or share with me the roadmap. That's an observation. It's a fact. I could take a picture of it, and no one would argue with it. The next step is feelings. So I'm going to express my feelings without blame. So I felt anxious not knowing what was on the roadmap for the week. I felt confused about whether that meeting happened or not because I wasn't included. So this is me sharing my feelings so the other party can empathize and understand what I'm going through without being defensive. (01:14:59): The third step is needs. What are my universal human needs related to this topic? We all have needs. This is not requiring anything of the other person, just helping them understand my needs that are not met. So I have a need for clarity, I have a need for collaboration, I have a need for connection, whatever that is. And lastly, the step is to make a request. Now, in this model, the request is an olive branch to help the other person meet you and see you. It shouldn't be something that's impossible to do. It should be actually something quite small and easy to achieve for the other person to feel successful in connecting to you and understanding you. So in this case, I might make a request. I'd like to ask you next time you have a sprint planning meeting to include me as optional or to send me the roadmap afterwards that you align on. (01:15:54): Now, the other person doesn't have to meet my request. They might make a counter proposal, but the most important thing of this model in this conversation is that the other person understands what I'm going through and they don't feel reactive so that we can have a mutual conversation about what's going on.
turns.zh: 首先，当人们想发生冲突、或想介入一件不顺的事时，他们是"披甲上阵"、准备好证明自己是对的。这很自然。你一直在想这件事，反复斟酌要不要提。你终于到了开口的节点，而常常有一种错误的观念，认为目标是说服对方他们做错了。实际上，任何冲突的目标都是达成相互理解。所以当我去找我丈夫谈——比如他没分担该做的育儿——我的目标是帮他理解我在挣扎什么，好让他能共情、看清发生了什么，并也许在某种程度上满足我的需求。但这不是为了向他证明他在家里做得有多少，因为他对自己身上发生的事，可能有一套完全不同的叙事。(01:13:54): 所以我要给你一个我喜欢的、很多客户都在用的框架。它来自 Marshall Rosenberg 的《非暴力沟通》（Nonviolent Communication）。那是一本书，也是一个框架。它有四步。第一步是观察（observations）。我的任务是记录事实层面发生了什么。例如，我注意到，在过去三次 sprint 规划会上，你没邀请我参加那些对话，也没和我分享路线图。那是一个观察。它是事实。我拍张照，没人会反驳它。第二步是感受（feelings）。我要不带指责地表达我的感受。所以，不知道这周路线图有什么，我感到焦虑。因为没被包括进去，我对那会到底开没开感到困惑。所以这是我分享我的感受，好让对方能够共情、理解我的处境，而不至于 defensive（防御）。(01:14:59): 第三步是需求（needs）。与这个话题相关的、我普遍的人类需求是什么？我们都有需求。这并不要求对方做什么，只是帮他们理解我的需求，而那……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. This point about how when you're trying to convince someone of something, when something is going wrong, this point that your goal is not to convince them, that your goal is to have mutual understanding, that just blew my mind, and I think it's going to change my life. Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。关于当你想说服别人某件事、当出了问题时，你的目标不是说服他们、而是达成相互理解——这一点简直让我醍醐灌顶，我觉得它会改变我的人生。哇。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Lenny, try this with your wife tonight. NVC is a powerful tool, and actually it's very akin to most models that are about connection. The Stanford Business School course that has a T, it's called Touchy Feely that everybody loves.
turns.zh: Lenny，今晚和你妻子试试这个。NVC 是个有力的工具，而且它其实和大多数关于连接的模型非常相似。斯坦福商学院有个课名里带个 T，叫 Touchy Feely，大家都爱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we've had Carol on the podcast.
turns.zh: 对，我们请过 Carol 上播客。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Great. Yeah, so Carol Robbins created this movement. There's lit. A lot of founders go to her model that's for founders.
turns.zh: 太好了。对，所以 Carol Robbins 创了这套东西。有文献。很多创始人去用她那套为创始人设计的模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And tech.
turns.zh: 还有科技圈。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And this is all about, they talk about a net that you can talk about your feelings and your reaction, but as soon as you cross the net to blaming someone else or making an assumption, they're going to have a defensive response. But you can be incredibly bold and brave if you stay on your side of the net. So this model helps you do that because it's really about sharing your emotions and your needs and making a request without blame.
turns.zh: 而这一切关乎：他们讲一张"网"，你可以谈你的感受和你自己的反应，但一旦你越过网去指责别人或做假设，对方就会防御性地回应。但如果你待在网自己这一边，你可以极其大胆、勇敢。所以这个模型帮你做到这点，因为它真正关乎分享你的情绪和你的需求，并在不指责的情况下提出请求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So what I was going to say as you were going through this framework is here's me, here's what I saw, here's what I'm feeling, here's what I need. And then now that you have that in context, here's something I'm asking for versus you did this and you're feeling this and you thought this.
turns.zh: 对。所以你过这个框架时，我想说的是：这是我，这是我所看到的，这是我的感受，这是我的需求。然后，在你有了这个语境之后，这是我请求的事——而不是"你做了这个、你感到这个、你想到这个"。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Exactly. It also acknowledges that professionals have feelings. I think that we operate in tech. We're supposed to give all of ourselves, all of our time, all of our energy to this endeavor. And it's purely logical. It's not at all true. It's completely emotional. And if we ignore our feelings, they will bubble up, and we will be unconsciously acting from them.
turns.zh: 正是。它也承认职场人是有感情的。我认为我们身处科技圈。我们本该把全部的自我、时间、能量都投入这项事业。而且它纯粹是理性的。但完全不是这样。它完全是感性的。而如果我们忽视自己的感受，它们会冒出来，我们就会在无意识中受它们驱动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's this implicit power here that if the person cares about you and loves you or values your relationship, knowing that this makes them feel bad will make them want to change. It's not like you need to tell them, "Change this thing. Oh, I didn't realize this made you upset or that you have this need. And now that I know that, okay, now I see why this is important to you."
turns.zh: 而这里有一种隐含的力量：如果那个人在乎你、爱你、或重视你们的关系，知道这让他们感到糟糕，就会让他们想要改变。你不需要告诉他们"改掉这事"。哦，我没意识到这让你难过，或者你有这个需求。而既然我现在知道了，好，我现在明白这对你为什么重要了。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: That's exactly right. And sometimes the other person will hear that and have a different story or a different perspective. So they might say, " Okay, I can honor that request," or, "I hear that request, and I hear your feelings, but let me explain what happened for me." And one way you could do that is, are you open to hearing that? So they're able to share their side too. You don't have to just agree with the person's request. As long as you're setting this tone, the other person's more likely to contribute in a way that achieves mutual understanding because once you're vulnerable, they're going to share their vulnerability.
turns.zh: 完全正确。而有时候对方听到这些，会有不同的故事或不同的视角。所以他们可能会说，"好，我可以尊重那个请求，"或者"我听到了那个请求，也听到了你的感受，但让我解释一下我这边发生了什么。"而你可以这样问：你愿意听我说那个吗？这样他们也能分享他们那一边。你不必只是同意对方的要求。只要你定下这个基调，对方就更可能以达成相互理解的方式参与进来，因为一旦你坦诚了，他们也会分享他们的坦诚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me remind folks of the framework. I'm going to try using this. I wish it was a handy acronym off. So the framework is share what you've observed, just the facts of what is happening. Just simply, I saw you didn't close the fridge fully. Your feelings of how that made you feel, the needs that your core human need that drives that feeling, I imagine. And then the request you have of the person.
turns.zh: 让我提醒大家一下这个框架。我要试着用它。真希望它有个顺口的缩写。所以框架是：分享你所观察到的，只是正在发生的事实。很简单，我看到你没把冰箱门关严。你的感受——那让你有什么感觉，驱动那感受的核心人类需求，我猜。然后是你对那个人的请求。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yes. And I want to make one note I forgot to say, which is feelings are emotions. So sometimes people say things like, "I feel like you're being a jerk." That's not a feeling, obviously. A feeling is a sensation in your body that results in an emotion. So naming a feeling is actually not easy for technical leaders sometimes. I want to make that point because emotions are what get you to the underlying humanity of connection. Emotions are the key to soliciting empathy.
turns.zh: 对。而且我想补一句我忘了说的：感受就是情绪。所以人们有时会说，"我觉得你是个混蛋。"那显然不是感受。感受是你身体里产生的一种感觉，进而成为情绪。所以对技术型领导者来说，说出一种感受有时并不容易。我想强调这一点，因为情绪才是把你带到连接之下的那份人性的东西。情绪是唤起共情的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there phrases that are just examples of non-feelings, like using the word "you" in the way you describe a feeling probably is not a good sign?
turns.zh: 有没有哪些措辞就是"非感受"的例子，比如你描述感受时用了"你"这个词，大概就不是好兆头？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Exactly. If you can say, "I feel like... " even if you add like or, "I feel that... " you're probably going to add a fact. It should be an emotion word after I feel.
turns.zh: 正是。如果你会说"我觉得……"即便加上 like，或者"我感觉……"你大概会接上一个事实。I feel 后面应该是个情绪词。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So don't say like, don't say you, don't say that?
turns.zh: 所以别说 like，别说 you，别说那个？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Along this topic, I chatted with a number of clients that have worked with you over the years, and one of the most common themes that they said you help them with is having difficult conversations. And I think we covered actually much of this in what we just talked about, but I'm curious if there's any other advice you have for helping people have difficult conversations. Let me read a quote from one of your clients.
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺着这个话题，我和多年来和你合作过的几位客户聊过，他们提到你帮他们最多的一个常见主题，就是进行艰难的对话。而我认为我们其实在刚才的对话里已经覆盖了很多，但我好奇，关于帮人们进行艰难对话，你还有没有别的建议。让我读一段你一位客户的话。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Oh, wow. I love this.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。我喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So she said, "Rachel is exceptional at making difficult decisions clear and making it feel possible to get these decisions actualized." Is there anything more-
turns.zh: 她说，"Rachel 特别擅长把艰难的决定变得清晰，并让人觉得这些决定是可以落地的。"还有没有别的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... these decisions actualized. Is there anything more there for, because difficult conversations are difficult. How do we help people make them less difficult? Any tips?
turns.zh: ……这些决定得以落地。关于这个还有没有更多可说的，因为艰难的对话之所以难，就是因为它难。我们怎么帮人们让它们没那么难？有什么技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. Well, first of all, difficult conversations makes you want to run away. The marketing on conflict is poor, so I want to reframe that. My belief is when we feel internally ambivalent, we have two inner parts at war. And there's something really beautiful and important to pay attention to, there's something to learn, when we have ambivalence. When we are in conflict, something important is at stake. We care deeply about what we're building, about the person that's letting us down. So the reason it's hard, is because there's such an emotional component to it. And there's something to learn from it. (01:21:57): So first, I want leaders who are listening to think, "This is hard, because I have something to learn here, and because it matters. So instead of avoiding it and running away, I'm going to lean into this moment. And I'm going to come out of it not just having solved this dynamic, and not just having said my piece, but having built a skill." The reason I focus on interpersonal dynamics is because the quality of our relationships determines the quality of our life. I really believe that. And if you cannot have conflict, you can't have healthy relationships. We are going to disagree with the people we love, or care about, or are building a business with. So first, I just want listeners to reframe ambivalence and interpersonal challenge, think of them as a growth opportunity. (01:22:56): Second, there is always something that we're doing to contribute to the conflict, even if it feels like the other person is insane, and is driving us crazy, and we're the innocent party. So entering any conflict conversation with humility, and curiosity about the other person's experience, is critical to setting the table for a commitment to come out better and stronger. So no model, NVC or otherwise, can fix a person who's coming in rigid and full of blame. I really love the 15 Commitments to Conscious Leaders, I don't know if you know that book, but one of the concepts is about taking a hundred percent responsibility. Not being in the world of blame, being a victim, or being a hero. And I see many leaders, when they're in a challenging interpersonal conflict, being in victimhood, being in blame, or being in hero. "I'm just going to do it for them, and forget it. They're having such a hard time getting this done, I'm just going to do it." (01:24:10): Instead, take responsibility for your part. "What is my piece in making this dynamic happen and how can I address it?"
turns.zh: 是的。首先，艰难的对话会让人想逃避。关于冲突的营销做得很糟糕，所以我想重新诠释这个概念。我的观点是，当我们内心感到矛盾时，内心有两个部分在交战。当我们感到矛盾时，总有一些重要的东西值得关注，有东西值得学习。这时候，我们需要直面冲突，深切关怀我们正在构建的事业，以及让我们失望的人。因此，之所以困难，是因为其中蕴含着情感因素。但我们能从中收获成长。（01:21:57）所以首先，我希望聆听的领导者们能思考：“这很困难，因为我能从中学习，也因为它至关重要。所以与其逃避和回避，不如直面当下，解决冲突，分享见解，最终掌握一项技能。” 我关注人际动态的原因在于，我们的人际关系质量决定着生活的质量。我深信这一点。如果没有冲突，就谈不上健康的人际关系。我们会与所爱之人、关心之人、共事之人产生分歧。因此，我希望听众能重新审视矛盾和人际挑战，将其视为成长的机会。（01:22:56）其次，即便对方看似不可理喻、令人抓狂，而我们自视无辜，我们的行为中也总有助长冲突的因素。因此，以谦逊之心和对他人经历的好奇心投入冲突对话，对达成共同成长至关重要。任何模式，无论是非暴力沟通还是其他方法，都无法改变那些带着僵化思维、满怀指责的人。我非常推崇《意识型领导者的15项承诺》，不知道你是否了解这本书，其中一条核心理念就是百分百承担责任。不要陷入指责的怪圈、受害者心态或英雄情结。我见过许多领导者在面临挑战性的人际冲突时，陷入受害者心态、指责他人或扮演英雄角色。“我来替他们做吧，他们做不到，我就来做。” （01:24:10）相反，要为自己的行为负责：“我在这段关系中起了什么作用？如何改进？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes me think about, Jerry Colonna was on the podcast, and he has this famous line that I've always remembered. How are you complicit in creating the conditions that you claim you don't want?
turns.zh: 这让我想到，杰瑞·科隆纳曾做客播客，他有一句让我印象深刻的话：你如何参与创造了自己声称不想要的环境？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yes, I love that. Love that question.
turns.zh: 是的，我很喜欢这个问题。很爱这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's so many, there's three parts to that whole question, I won't get into it. But what you're sharing here is, think about that, figure out how, because your point is, you're always somehow complicit in creating the issue you're complaining about. And use that to help kind of put down the defense of the person like, "Here's what I've contributed to this problem." Do you use the nonviolent communication framework? And I don't know, is that just a general way of trying to have difficult conversations, or is there not a framework?
turns.zh: 这个问题有三个层面，我就不展开了。但你分享的观点是，思考这一点，找出原因，因为你的观点是，你总是在某种程度上参与了你所抱怨的问题的产生。然后用这个来帮助消除对他人的防御，比如说：“以下是我对这个问题的贡献。” 你使用非暴力沟通框架吗？我不知道，这是不是一种进行艰难对话的通用方法，还是没有框架？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, no, I think that's a great framework for when you want to go interact with someone around something that's not working for you. I think typically a difficult conversation arises because some feelings are coming up for you, and you have a need that's not being met. And so, that's the instigator to know, "Okay, I need to talk to this person. We need to clear this up." (01:25:17): For example, I was working with a CEO whose co-founder was constantly undercutting his decisions, and criticizing him. And there was something happening, where they'd gone from being this great dynamic duo, fundraised, hired a few leaders, and then all of a sudden he was getting daggers thrown at him all the time. And it was exhausting, and frustrating, and confusing. That was a time where he used NVC to address, "What is happening, here?" And it turned out that the co-founder was really frustrated with how he was spending his time. He didn't want him to be off selling, he wanted him to be helping him with product vision. And they had a totally different conception of how the CEO should be spending his time.
turns.zh: 是的，不，我觉得当你想就某件对自己不利的事与他人沟通时，这个沟通框架很棒。我认为通常艰难的对话之所以产生，是因为你内心涌现了某些情绪，而你的某种需求未被满足。因此，关键在于要意识到：“好吧，我需要和这个人谈谈。我们得把这事理清楚。” （01:25:17）：例如，我曾与一位CEO合作，他的联合创始人总是贬低他的决策，批评他。起初，他们是绝佳的搭档，成功融资，招募了几位高管，但突然间对方对他充满恶意。这令人精疲力竭、沮丧又困惑。就在那时，他运用非暴力沟通技巧探寻：“到底发生了什么？” 结果发现联合创始人对CEO的时间分配方式极为不满。他不希望CEO外出销售，而是希望CEO协助制定产品愿景，而他们对CEO应如何分配时间有着截然不同的理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Just remind folks of the NVC framework, because this is the thing that's hard in the moment. Like, "Oh, what should I be saying?" Observe, feelings, needs, request.
turns.zh: 太棒了。再提醒大家注意非暴力沟通框架，因为这在当下确实很难。比如，“我该说些什么？”观察情绪、需求、请求。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And there's a nonviolent communication book, if folks are into the framework, and want to check it out.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。如果大家对这个框架感兴趣，可以去看看相关书籍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People need a little... Who was it, you said one of your client's tattooed the vision he had, on-
turns.zh: 人们需要一点……谁来着？你说你的一位客户把他的愿景纹在身上了，对吧？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, there's, let's just get something.
turns.zh: 好的，我们先找个东西。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Maybe don't tattoo NVC.
turns.zh: 或许别纹非暴力沟通术语。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because that may be [inaudible 01:26:25]
turns.zh: 因为那样可能不太合适。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: It doesn't have a good acronym. You could just print it out, and put it right next to your screen, or something-
turns.zh: 这个术语没有好的缩写。你可以把它打印出来，放在屏幕旁边，或者——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, okay.
turns.zh: 好的，好的。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: ... if you want.
turns.zh: ……如果你愿意的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No tattoos. I just want to highlight the first point you made in this answer, of having difficult conversations. And then I have one more question for you. Just this point about, if there's something you're afraid of, that is a sign you should do that. There's a quote I often think of. "The cave you fear contains the treasure you seek." And the advice there is just, the thing you're afraid of is a compass too, the thing you should do. Because there's something important there.
turns.zh: 别纹身。我只想强调你在这段回答中提到的第一个要点，即如何进行艰难的对话。接下来我还有一个问题要问你。如果你害怕某件事，那就说明你应该去做这件事。我常想起一句名言：“你害怕的那个洞穴，里面藏着你要寻找的宝藏。” 这里的建议是：你害怕的东西，也能指引你该做的事。因为那里藏着重要的东西。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I love that. Yeah. It's like, "What's important here? What do I have to learn here?" Is a question you can ask yourself when you're avoiding something. I often see this in talent management situations. A CEO has an underperforming COO. They're avoiding a conversation, because they keep getting let down, and actually they kind of know deep down, this is not working out. They don't want to face it. It's too much work. They need to just keep plowing forward. (01:27:27): And when we really take space to think about their feelings and needs, they realize, I ask them, "Would you enthusiastically rehire this person for the same role?" Which is the question we always asked at Stripe. And when the answer is no to that, no matter how many difficult conversations you have, this is not going to work. So then you have to take action. And even engaging in the hard conversation, and seeing what happens, can lead you to the clarity that you need to take action on talent that's not working.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样做。是啊。这就像在问：“这里最重要的是什么？我需要在这里学到什么？” 当你逃避某件事时，你可以问自己这个问题。我在人才管理中经常看到这种情况。CEO手下有个表现不佳的COO。他们回避谈话，因为一次次失望，实际上他们内心深处也知道这行不通，但他们不愿面对现实。太麻烦了，他们只想继续埋头苦干。（01:27:27）：当我们真正花时间思考他们的感受和需求时，他们会意识到，我会问他们：“你会热情地重新雇用这个人担任同样的角色吗？” 这正是我们在Stripe一直问的问题。当答案是否定的，无论你进行了多少次艰难的谈话，这段关系都注定失败。所以你必须采取行动。即使参与艰难的对话，看看结果，也能让你清楚地知道该如何处理不达标的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really cool tip. I did not know Stripe operated that way. We had the CTO of Netflix on the podcast, Elizabeth Stone, and this is very much how they operate. They're always asking a question like that. The way you phrased it was, "Would I enthusiastically rehire this person for the same role?"
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的建议。我不知道Stripe是这样运作的。我们在播客上邀请了Netflix的CTO伊丽莎白·斯通，他们的运作方式也非常相似。他们总是问这样一个问题。你刚才描述的方式是：“你会热情地重新雇用这个人担任同样的角色吗？”

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Exactly. It's very clarifying, because it's binary. People have a physical sense, just like we talked about a full body yes, before? You have a immediate reaction that is honest, to that question, that provides clarity.
turns.zh: 没错。这很清晰，因为这是二选一的问题。人们有直观的感觉，就像我们之前讨论的全身心投入的“是”吗？面对这个问题，你会立即做出诚实的反应，这能带来清晰的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the answer isn't, if it's no, it's not, "Fire them." It's, "You need to do something about it." It could be talk to them about it, put them on a performance plan, put them in a different role. It doesn't mean you have to fire them immediately, so it's not necessarily as scary as it sounds, if you say no.
turns.zh: 如果答案是否定的，并不意味着要立即解雇他们。这意味着你需要采取行动。比如和他们谈谈，制定绩效计划，或者让他们转岗。这并不意味着必须立即解雇，所以如果答案是否定的，并不像听起来那么可怕。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, I think that also it depends on the stage of business you're in. So I see a lot of companies build a leadership team, and then a year later, the size and stage of their business is dramatically different. And they start to realize, "Oh, the CFO that was really fine back then, is now completely wrong. He should be the controller." Okay, great. So reckon with that. Recognize that in how you're interacting with your current CFO, put out a search. There's many things you can do that aren't firing someone. But in quickly scaling businesses, it's natural that the leadership team's job will change, and that you'll have to make some evolution over time.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这也取决于你所处的业务阶段。我看到很多公司组建了领导团队，一年后，他们的业务规模和阶段就发生了巨大变化。他们开始意识到：“哦，当时还不错的CFO现在完全不合适了。他应该去当财务总监。” 好的，没问题。所以要正视这个问题。认识到你在与现任CFO互动时存在的问题，启动人才搜寻。还有很多不涉及解雇的办法。但在快速扩张的企业中，领导团队的职责自然会发生变化，你必须随着时间推移进行调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I guess it's very important to highlight the importance of operating this way, if you're trying to build a really successful company, is that should be the bar. Is, if you would not enthusiastically rehire this person for this role. If you're trying to build something that's never been built before, and build a company that actually works out really well, you need to really only have people around that are hitting that bar.
turns.zh: 我想，如果你想建立一家真正成功的公司，强调以这种方式运作的重要性非常重要。这应该成为标准。就是，如果你不会热情地重新雇用这个人担任这个角色。如果你想打造前所未有的产品，建立一家真正成功的公司，你就只需要身边有符合这个标准的人。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. My perspective, I talked at the beginning about how I'm obsessed with the human side of business building, and my belief is that talent and the environment that you put your talent in is everything. Yes. Building a product and a business is about building something that users need. It's about product market fit, and then the wave you're on. Timing is important. You're going to build a different size business, if you're in a sector that's not growing, than right now, if you're in the middle of AI. True. You're riding a timing wave, and you're solving a core need. But everything besides that is so human. It's about talent, and it's about the environment that you put that talent in. So you need to create the conditions such that your talent can thrive.
turns.zh: 是的。以我的观点来看，我在开头提到过，我痴迷于商业构建中的人性化层面，我坚信人才及其所处的环境至关重要。没错，打造产品和企业就是要满足用户的需求。这关乎产品与市场的契合度，以及你所处的时代浪潮。时机很重要。如果你身处一个停滞不前的行业，所能建立的企业规模与当下人工智能领域的企业相比就相形见绌。确实，你正顺势而为，满足核心需求。但除此之外，一切都关乎人性——人才及其所处的环境。因此，你需要创造条件，让人才能够蓬勃发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a simple concept, that I think people overlook, is just everything you do is going to be the people that you have around you, and the environment you create for them to operate. I think your point about when you're doing something difficult, just to close out this element, I love this idea that if it feels hard, think of it as a learning opportunity. I think anyone listening to this is like, "Oh, cool, I'm going to learn something. I'm going to get better." It's such a easier, more motivating way of approaching something that's difficult.
turns.zh: 有一个被人们忽视的简单概念：你所做的一切都离不开身边的人，以及你为他们创造的运作环境。关于克服困难的部分，我想强调一点：当你面临挑战时，把它视为学习的机会。听众会觉得：“哦，太棒了，我要学点新东西，提升自己。”这种以更积极、更具激励性的方式应对挑战，远比强迫自己忍受枯燥的工作要容易得多。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: And I want to make a distinction between that and what we talked about earlier, which was, lean into your strengths. Because I don't believe people should suffer through the day grinding, doing work that's depleting. That's not a learning opportunity. Interpersonally, when you're avoiding something, it's because you care about something. Avoiding your emotions is what I want to encourage people against. We have to feel our feelings all the way through, be present to our feelings, and interact with others in a way that acknowledges our feelings. That's what I want to encourage, because actually that's not deadening, that's enlivening. And there's learning there.
turns.zh: 这里我要区分一下和之前提到的"发挥自身优势"。我的观点是，人们不应在枯燥的工作中煎熬，因为那并非学习的机会。人际交往中，当你回避某件事时，往往是因为你在乎某些东西。我希望人们不要压抑自己的情绪。我们需要直面内心的感受，坦然面对情绪，并以尊重情感的方式与他人互动。这才是我所倡导的，因为这种方式不仅不令人麻木，反而能激发活力，并在其中收获成长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A final area I want to spend a little time on is, something that I've heard from everybody that you work with, which is the way that you help them operate. So you just talked about the importance of the people you hire and the environment you create for them. And something that you help leaders do is create a very specific way of operating around a one-page plan, and how that kind of trickles down and just makes everything at a company more effective. Talk about this one-page plan, how you recommend companies operate with this.
turns.zh: 最后我想谈谈一个关键点——我从合作过的每个人那里都听到过，你们如何帮助他们高效运作。你们刚刚提到招募人才的重要性以及为他们创造的环境。你们还帮助领导者围绕一页计划建立特定的运作方式，这种方式如何层层渗透，让整个公司的运作更加高效。能否谈谈这种一页计划，以及你们如何建议企业以此运作？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, thanks for asking that question. I think, typically, companies have complicated the process of aligning their vision, their strategy, their goals, and the way people behave with each other, their values. So that all of these things live in different places, are talked about to a different degree, resonate to employees differently. And if you asked anyone at the company, "What are your top three priorities, and how do they relate to the vision?" It's not an easy answer. (01:32:50): So the reason I like the one-page plan concept is, it's simplifying. It's a way for the leadership team to come together and align around, " What are we doing here? What is our role in it? And how do we communicate it, so that the whole company has clarity, and knows how the work they're doing ladders up to our big picture vision that we're all committed to?" (01:33:14): So I actually got this idea of the one-page plan from Alpine Investors. They have something called the People First Operating Rhythm, and they've successfully implemented that at their portfolio companies. And I work in concert with Alpine, so I work with some of their portfolio CEOs. To execute this rhythm. So it's not just about a one-page plan. It puts your vision and your values on the first column, your strategic intentions and your KPIs on the second column, your annual goals on the third, and your quarterly goals on the fourth. So that no matter what you're talking about, in terms of, "What are we doing for the next year, or the next quarter? How do we prioritize?" It's always in tandem with your core KPIs, your strategy, and your vision. (01:34:04): And I love how they instituted that with their portfolio, and I saw the power of it. They've collected some data that their portfolio companies that actually institute the People First Operating Rhythm result in higher returns. So they're very committed to this strategy, and after operating with CEOs in their rhythm, I took some of those ideas and started to help other founders and other leaders with some of the same concepts, in my own way.
turns.zh: 是的，感谢你提出这个问题。我认为通常来说，公司会让愿景、战略、目标以及员工间相互协作的方式、价值观等各方面变得复杂。因此，这些元素往往各自为政，讨论程度不一，对员工的触动也各不相同。如果你问公司里的任何人，“你们的三大优先事项是什么，它们与公司的愿景有何关联？”答案往往并不容易。（01:32:50）所以我喜欢单页计划的理念，是因为它能简化流程。它让领导团队能聚焦共识：“我们在这里做什么？我们在其中扮演什么角色？又该如何传达这些，让全公司都清晰明了自己的工作如何与我们共同坚守的宏伟愿景相契合？” （01:33:14）实际上，我是从Alpine Investors那里获得单页计划的灵感的。他们推行“以人为先的运营节奏”，并成功地在其投资组合公司中实施了这一理念。我与Alpine密切合作，协助部分投资组合公司的CEO们执行这一节奏。它不仅仅是单页计划。它将愿景和价值观放在第一列，战略意图和关键绩效指标放在第二列，年度目标放在第三列，季度目标放在第四列。因此，无论你讨论的是明年或下一季度的工作重点，还是资源分配优先级，都能与核心KPI、战略和愿景紧密结合。（01:34:04）我很欣赏他们在投资组合公司中推行这一做法，并见证了其成效。他们收集的数据显示，采用“以人为先的运营节奏”的投资组合公司获得了更高的回报。因此，他们对这一策略非常重视。在与CEO们共同实践后，我将其中的一些理念融入自己的工作方式，帮助其他创始人和领导者应用类似的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to hopefully link to a template of this one-page plan?
turns.zh: 我们希望能链接到这个单页计划的模板吗？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, sure.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Happy to share.
turns.zh: 很乐意分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let's do that. And then, what kind of impact do you see from companies starting to operate this way to motivate people to do this?
turns.zh: 好的，那我们就这么做吧。那么，你认为公司开始以这种方式运作，对激励人们这样做有什么样的影响？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah. What I see is clarity and alignment. And I also see more connection. So I want to name that it's not just about having a plan, it's about how you create it, how you reflect on it, and how you come together around it to celebrate wins. (01:34:57): So in my opinion, a very under- attended to part of building a business is an operating rhythm. When do you come together to kick off the year, and share your strategy and vision again, and talk about the goals? When do you come together to reflect on what's working and not working, and how do you do that? And in what groups? And are you honest, or are you just kind of doing it as a quick exercise to move on to what's pressing? (01:35:25): So just like I said in co-founder dynamics, a key is to step out of the dance floor and to get onto the balcony. Executive teams leading a complex business need time away from being in the business to work on the business. So around this one-page plan, the reason I like a rhythm, is you can kick off the year with the plan. That's really simple, easy to understand. Everyone can have it accessible and every quarter, you can get together to reflect, "What worked, what didn't work?" (01:35:56): I really like the question, "What's an inconvenient truth?" Air the things that need to be talked about, that no one's talking about because you're too busy. That's the power of combining a simple plan, whether it's one page or not, that aligns you from the top to the bottom, your vision all the way down to your quarterly goals. And a time where you stop, pause, discuss, reflect, have a little spacious energy. (01:36:26): It's not unlike what you said about your own time. You are the executive team. You want a little bit of spacious time to tinker, reflect, create, and come back to the meaningful work you're doing more energized. And leadership teams need that too.
turns.zh: 是的。我看到的是清晰的思路和目标一致性。我还看到了更紧密的协作。所以我想强调的是，成功不仅在于制定计划，更在于如何制定计划、如何反思计划，以及如何围绕计划团结一致，共同庆祝成功。（01:34:57）：在我看来，构建企业过程中一个常被忽视的关键环节是运营节奏。何时齐聚一堂，开启新的一年，再次分享战略愿景，探讨目标？何时停下来反思哪些措施有效，哪些尚需改进？又该在何种场合进行反思？是坦诚面对，还是草草了事，以便继续处理紧急事务？（01:35:25）：正如我在联合创始人动态中所说，关键在于跳出舞池，登上阳台。领导复杂业务的管理团队需要抽离业务本身，专注于业务本身。因此围绕这份一页计划书，我青睐这种节奏——年初以计划为开端。这既简单明了，易于理解，每个季度又能借此回顾总结：哪些措施奏效，哪些尚待改进？（01:35:56）：我特别喜欢“令人不适的真相”这个问题。把那些因忙碌而无人提及的难题暴露于光下。正是简单计划（无论是否为一页计划）的力量，将从上到下的愿景与季度目标紧密相连，让人们得以停下脚步、暂停反思、激发灵感，再以更充沛的精力投入到有意义的工作中。这与你提到的个人时间管理理念不谋而合。你作为管理团队成员，需要片刻静思、反思、创造，再以更充沛的精力投入到高效工作中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, Alpine Investors, Graham Weaver. He was on the podcast.
turns.zh: 等等，Alpine Investors，Graham Weaver。他上过播客。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: I saw that. I saw that.
turns.zh: 我看到了。我看到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay, final, final question. I want to take us to AI corner before we get to the very exciting lighting round. I'm going to do kind of a tweaked version. Usually I ask people just, how has AI impacted their work and life? I guess that is the question here, just how has AI changed, I guess coaching, as a coach? But also just, from a client's perspective, how are people using AI to help them in their, I guess life, from a coaching perspective?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。好，最后一个问题。最后一个问题。在进入激动人心的提问环节之前，我想先聊聊AI相关的话题。我会稍作调整。通常我会问人们AI如何影响他们的工作和生活。我猜这里的问题是，AI如何改变了教练的工作，尤其是从客户视角来看，他们如何利用AI辅助生活？

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. So as a coach, I use AI in a couple of key ways, that I'm grateful for. One, I use Granola, which I saw you give away to your listeners.
turns.zh: 是的，这是个很棒的问题。作为教练，我在几个关键方面运用AI，这让我心怀感激。首先，我使用Granola，我看到你把它送给听众了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One free year of Granola, for becoming an annual subscriber of Lenny's Newsletter, lennysnewsletter.com.
turns.zh: 免费使用Granola一年，仅限订阅Lenny's Newsletter的用户，订阅请访问lennysnewsletter.com。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: There you go. (01:37:29): So I use Granola to take notes in our session so I can be fully present with my clients, and I can give them a synthesis of what happened and the next steps they committed to after our session. I also use it, I put them in a folder for every client, and so I can look at insights across our work together. What are the deeper things that are happening? What are the patterns that are taking place? I have these in my head, but actually it's a great tool, to see over time. "Oh yeah, we talked about that in our first session. Let's bring that back, because that's what you're struggling with now." So it helps me create the kind of transformation that I want for all my clients. (01:38:08): Secondly, I just use ChatGPT to help me plan my retreats. I run a women's organization, and we have eight retreats a year, and it's a great tool to think expansively about new activities. Once I've gotten the core objectives down, and I have a bunch of ideas about what I want to do, it gives me new creative ideas. So I can put in like, "Here's my objective, here's my goal, here's my audience, here's my last retreat that I ran. I kind of want three new ideas for this session." So it'll give me creative energy that I otherwise would need to get together with other coaches to discuss. And I do that, too. (01:38:50): Finally, I'm experimenting with AI in a way to support my clients between sessions. So I've gotten some feedback from my clients that they would like more interaction between our sessions, and they're always allowed to email me, or text me. I'm available to them. But I think they want to be really respectful of my time, and so some people do reach out and ask me questions, and other people wait for our session. (01:39:17): So I'm curious about the future of coaching, how in between sessions, clients can get access to more of an AI support, where the bot has all of their context, their development plan that we create at the beginning. So that's their goals, for our work together, how they want to grow. Some of my core frameworks, and my beliefs, and my training. And the Granola notes from all of our sessions, so that they can access between, just some extra spot support. They're going into this conversation, how should they approach it? They're anxious about this team meeting. How can they make the most of it? More tactical support. I see personal coaching as still critical for, "What is your vision of your life? How do you want to shift your core behavior to align with that vision?" But then, AI can play a real helpful role in between, on the tactics.
turns.zh:
好的。（01:37:29）所以我在我们的会面中使用Granola来做笔记，这样我就能全心专注于客户，并向他们汇总会面内容和下一步行动。我还会把这些笔记整理成每个客户的文件夹，这样就能回顾我们共同成长的历程。哪些深层问题正在浮现？哪些模式正在显现？这些问题在我脑海中挥之不去，但Granola这个工具能让我随着时间推移清晰观察进展。“哦对了，我们第一次会面时谈过这个问题。现在该把它重新提出来了，因为这正是你当前面临的挑战。”这有助于我为所有客户创造理想的成长转变。  
（01:38:08）其次，我用ChatGPT来规划静修活动。作为女性组织的运营者，我们每年举办八次静修活动。这款工具能激发我对新活动的创意构想。一旦确定核心目标并收集了灵感，它会为我注入新创意。我会输入：“这是我的目标、受众，以及我上次举办的静修活动。我需要为这次活动获得三个新创意。”这样既能激发灵感，又省去了与其他教练反复探讨的时间。不过我也会和同事们交流想法。  
（01:38:50）最后，我正在尝试利用AI工具支持客户的会间互动。有些客户希望在会间获得更多支持，但又不想过度占用我的时间。他们可以随时发邮件或发短信联系我。但我发现他们更倾向于尊重我的个人时间。因此，有些人会主动提问，而另一些则等到正式会面时再交流。  
（01:39:17）我对未来教练服务充满期待，希望AI能在会间为客户提供更个性化的支持。例如，机器人可以存储客户的所有背景信息、我们共同制定的发展计划、他们的成长目标、我的核心框架和培训内容，以及所有会面记录。这样客户就能随时获取额外支持，应对各种挑战：比如如何准备一场会议？如何充分利用团队会议？这些都是实战性的支持。我始终认为个人指导至关重要，比如“你对生活的愿景是什么？如何调整核心行为以匹配这个愿景？”但AI能在会间策略层面提供有力支持。

turns.speaker: Rachel Lockett
turns.en: What I want to share is that the world is getting more lonely. So I am a fan of this AI boom, I appreciate that we have more technology at our fingertips than ever before. But I want to encourage listeners to think of themselves as leaders who bring humans together to self-actualize, and that they have to actively overcome the default state, which is blind, grind, and loneliness. So I think this is a call to action for your listeners, to connect with the people around them, lead healthier teams, create environments where connection is inevitable. turns.zh: 我书桌上有一句话。我很喜欢。准备好了吗？“如果你能看到你面前铺好的道路，一步一步，那就不是你的路。你自己的路，是你每走一步就创造出来的。这就是为什么它是你的路。”这是约瑟夫·坎贝尔说的。
